Public School Examination. The examination of the public schools which has been in progress since last Monday concluded yesterday with Prof. J. E. Skinner's department in school No. 2. Church Robbers. We learn that somebody forcibly entered the Christian Church in Georgetown by one of the windows a few days since, drank up the wine used for sacramental purposes and appropriated several articles of small value. Some one also entered Christ's Church in this city, the first of the week, but took nothing away with them. Brutal Treatment. From the Carlisle Mercury we copy the following, which is any thing but creditable if true: "After the races of Chester Park, Cincinnati, Jim Murphy, a well-known horseman from Lexington, Ky., the owner of the famous race horse Bob Hooley, outrageously beat a little colored boy, Oscar Johnson, fourteen years old, who has been in his employ. Murphy struck ex-Gov. Pinchback, of La., because he remonstrated. Warrendale Commencement.
Warrendale Commencement.

The commencement exercises of Warren-dale Seminary, Georgetown, came off at the Court House on Friday morning last. Every seat in the Court room where the exercises were held was filled by a large and attentive audience. A varied and attractive programme was presented, and the exercises were highly creditable to all who took part in the same, and to the institution represented. The graduates were Misses Bryan, Wolfe and Pryor.

A Disappointed Bridegroom.

A gentleman of this city who has not been married any great length of time, had occasion to go to Eastern Kentucky on some business connected with a coal mining company. He hastened home on Thursday to find his bride gone on a visit to a relative some distance off, with strict injunctions that he was not to follow. His friends leared for some days that he would come to harm, so keen was his disappointment. But he returned to his mine yesterday a sadder if not a wiser man.

New Biographical Dictionary.

An excellent feature of the New Edition of Webster's Unabridged Dictionary, just issued, is the New Biographical Dictionary, in which are given the names of nearly ten thousand noted persons of ancient and modern times, with a brief statement of the dates of their birth and death, their nationality, profession, etc. This is designed for purposes of ready reference, to answer the questions which often arise as to when and where certain persons lived, and the character of their achievements. It contains many names of persons who are still living and the pronunciation of each name is given.

Big Rivers.

The recent rains will give us booming rivers. The Ohio is higher at Pittsburg than at any time since 74, and apprehensions are felt of a dangerous flood. This will bring out all the coal that is mined, and tend materially to reduce the price, which dealers had determined to keep up if possible. The case in the money markets have enabled the coal men to hold their stocks and force consumers to pay extreme prices, but this flood will upset their calculations and bring down all the coal that is dug. If consumers will hold off they will get coal at reasonable figures.

Killing in Bath.

On Sunday morning last Anderson Johnson shot and killed Isaac Alfredy, in Bath county, near Licking Union church. The parties were consins, lived on adjoining farms, and had an altercation about Alfredy hogs which were continually getting into Johnson's corn field, and there was no effort being made to keep them out. When Alfredy was killed he had shot one shot at Johnson with a pistol, and was in the act of shooting again. Alfredy's son was also present, armed with a pistol; but Johnson leveled the other barrel of his shot-gun on him and commanded him to put up his weapon.

Elopement.

Elopement.

Last Tuesday Mr. Richard Brand, who resides near Broadwell's X Roads in this county, brought his handsome daughter, Miss Fannie B. Brand to this city, and placed her on the cars en route to Millersburg, where she was going to attend the Female College Commencement. At Shawhan's Station Miss Brand met Mr. Sidney Dills, a farmer residing in the eastern part of this county. The two passed on up to Lexington, and there took the Cincinnati Southern Rail Road for Cincinnati, where they arrived in safety, and putting up at the Burnett House; where they sent for a preacher, and were immediately united the bonds of matrimony.—Cynthiana News.

The Tin Box Trial.

The trial of the case of P. F. Maguire vs. the Fayette National Bank has been in progress since Tuesday, and has absorbed more attention than any civil suit ever did in Lexington. Nothing was developed which was not known to the public before. Some of the small vices and peccadillos of the young men of the town were ventilated, but nothing of a startling or criminal nature was developed. We refrain from publishing the testimony, as it can have but little interest for those who already know the main facts in the case. It was expected that it would close yesterday afternoon, but up to a late hour the court and lawyers were still wrestling with the vexatious litigation.

Bad Outlook.

A telegram from Chicago says "a leading commission house in that city has received reports from more than one hundred and fifty correspondents in the spring wheat States regarding the acreage sown to spring wheat this year as compared with last. The average of these reports, thus far, show the following percentages: Wisconsin, 81, Minnesota, 90; Iowa, 100; Nebraska, 100; Dakota, a large increase."

"Information received from Southern Illinois agreed in describing the outlook there as a poor one. Some fields owe their green appearance, not to wheat, but to cheat."

\ reliable gentleman from Richmond, Ind., "says a manufacturer of agricultural implements informed him that he could make more money by stopping work than by filling his orders, as many farmers were willing give $30 to $50 each to be relieved from their contracts to pay for reapers, &c."

Tricycling.

Tricycling has become a fashionable pursuit of the young men in England, and as the ladies never fail to follow in the wake of fashion when set by their admirers, the tricycle has been adopted by them with the greatest eagerness. At first it was considered "rather fast," and looked upon with shyness, but ever since the newspaper account of the ride taken by her Majesty and the Princess Beatrice, each royal lady mounted on her iron horse and careering gayly on the high road and through the green lanes round Osborne, all scruple has banished. It is urged that no danger can exist, as the Queen, who is a heavy, fat old lady, was enabled to sit her steed with as much ease and confidence as when in former days she used to prance so proudly on her high mettled horse before the troops at review. And so professors of the bicycle and tricycle abound in London, and the racing and chasing along the suburban roads at twilight and the laughing and chatting as the iron coursers shoot by, give quite a new aspect to the solitary walks round London.

SUNBEAMS.
The British Government will soon include a Minister of Agriculture.

The English "Rational Dress Society" has its model costume on view in London.

Sunday free concerts are given on Boston Common, at the city's expense, and there seems to be no serious objection.

Rosa Bonheur is at work on a grand study of some lions she kept in her grounds last summers and then gave to the Paris "Zoo."

A single robber stopped a stage near San Antonio, Texas, and riffled the mail bag, while four well armed passengers sat idly looking on.

Not many tourists go to shed tears on the tomb of Washington, and the managers of Mount Vernon propose to open a deer park as an attraction.

Jew boys are preferred to any others as office boys by numbers of Christians in New York. They are found to be exceptionally intelligent and trustworthy.

It is said that the check given by the Pennsylvania Railroad Company in payment for the Philadelphia, Wilmington and Baltimore road, $14,940,052 was the largest ever drawn in this country.

An effort is being made to have the presence of Queen Victoria at the opening of the New Dock Works at Leith in July. The ground has been entirely reclaimed from the sea, and the extension, when completed, will have cost £375,000.

A stranger walked down the main street of Vincennes, Ind., wearing a grotesque hat. Tom Boyes made fun of it. "Perhaps you'd like to shoot it," the wearer remarked. Tom responded with a pistol shot, which missed the hat and killed the man.
—Clara Folz, the San Francisco woman lawyer, being told by the opposing counsel in court that a woman's proper place was at home raising children, retorted: "A woman had better be engaged in almost any business than raising such men as you are, sir."

—Isaac Alfrey's dog bit Anderson Johnson's hog, at Owingsville, Ky. Then Johnson shot Alfrey's dog. Next, Alfrey shot Johnson's hog. Finally, Johnson shot Alfrey, killing him, and the latest report said that a mob had gone to hang the murderer.

—Josephine D'Orme, an Italian woman claiming the title of Countess of Caroli, recently died a domestic servant in San Francisco. She went to that city in 1863 as prima donna of the Blanche opera company, but lost her voice, and dropped into poverty and obscurity.

—Councilman Gallagher of Philadelphia keeps a resort of so bad a character that a movement was made to force him out of office. He voluntarily resigned, saying: "The odium that attaches to a Councilman does not make it a desirable place to be in for a man who has his living to make."

—Common Councils throughout the country are now dealing with the question whether to appropriate money for Fourth of July fireworks. The decision in most of the large cities of the East is generally in the negative, but in the West the popular demand for old-fashioned displays is too strong to be resisted.

—An advertiser in a Washington newspaper wants a position in any of the Government departments, and offers one-third of his salary for the place. Another says: "Will give any one $50 and 10 per cent for the first four months who will get me work in any of the departments at a salary of from $60 to $75 per month."

—"E. B." writes to the Wine and Spirit Review that while eminent divines like Dr. Howard Crosby assert that the wines of the Gospel were real fermented wines, fourth or fifth rate divines, on the other hand, are unable so to read the sacred book. Meanwhile "the Creator himself quietly smiles," &c. This correspondent seems to have exceptional information.

—A young woman was found shooting at a mark with a pistol in Fairmount Park, Philadelphia. A policeman asked her what she was doing that for, and she replied that she was practising preparatory to the murder of her recreant lover. She proved to be Georgianna Price, an actress. In court she reiterated her purpose, adding that she also meant to kill herself.

—Perhaps the most noticeable incident of the recent royal levee in London, says the London World, was old Admiral Sartorius—he is 92—going past with his two sons on their appointment to the Victoria Cross. There is only one other man in England who can boast such a chevron on his escutcheon, and that is Col. Hugh Gough, who also has two sons possessing each a V. C.

—All the musical notabilities of Belgium and many from abroad were present at the Liszt festival at Antwerp on May 27. Liszt congratulated the vocalists as well as the instrumentalists. At the invitation of the Burgomaster he wrote his name in the Golden Book of the city of Antwerp. The festival closed with the Preludes Symphoniques, which are considered one of Liszt's most successful compositions.

—The best known person in Florence is old Mr. Livingston of New York, who is strapped on to his box—having not long since tumbled off—while he drives his twenty bays glittering with gorgeous harness. The only occupant of the drag, except two solenin grooms, is usually a small barking dog. The whole thing suggests that passage in Swift's sermons: "We see, my friends, what God thinks of riches by the hands in which the places them."

—Benjamin P. Benner delivered a rousing address at a Grand Army gathering in Philadelphia, and his oratory astonished those among his hearers who knew that he had never shown any ability in that direction before. In the evening of the same day, Gen. Louis Wagner spoke at Scranton, and repeated Benner's language exactly. An investigation showed that Benner had got hold of a printed slip of the General's speech, and committed it to memory.

—Three negroes of Locksburg, Ark., were mistaken in supposing that a traveller, whom they were terrying across the river, carried a large amount of money, for, after murdering him, they found only $1 in his pockets. But nobody lived within several miles, and they felt no fear of detection after throwing the weighted remains into the stream. That was a second mistake, for a freshet occurred suddenly, and the remains were washed ashore by the force of the current. A third mistake was in believing that no great effort would be made to capture them, their victim having no friends in that region. A party of mounted lynchers chased them three days, and hanged them without trial.

—The particulars of the escape of Billy the Kid from Fort Stanton, Colorado, prove him as bold as he is bad. He is only 21, slight and boyish in looks, but hardened in villainy, being guilty of numerous murders. He was under sentence of death for one of these crimes. His casual remark, "I shan't be there at the hanging," led to the precaution of shackling him heavily, and placing two armed guards over him. While alone with one of these Billy fellled him with a blow of the manacles, and then killed him with his own pistol. The other guard was easily shot on his approach to the house. The desperado then filed off his irons, mounted a horse, and rode away in full view of a hundred men, whom he defied to interfere.

Some years ago an estate in Bedfordshire, England, reverted to the Crown. It had been previously held by Lord Dynevor, and then by the trustees of his estate, and in both cases the tenants made no complaint. The Crown agent, however, is averred to have "put on the screw," and the tenants, far from finding the increased indulgence they expected, have been so oppressed that one of them, an elderly man, lately killed himself. A razor was found near him, and on the table a paper in his handwriting bearing the words: "Old Mr. Chilton (the agent) is my murderer." The royal family personally have nothing whatever to do with the Crown estates, which are managed in the interest of the public by the Commissioners of Woods and Forests, who pay over the proceeds to the Treasury.

There was an extraordinary attendance at Christie & Manson's auction rooms in London on May

28, and the prizes at which certain pictures were sold were not less extraordinary. Two of Sir Edwin Landseer's works brought 5,000 guineas each, a third, 6,200 guineas. Concerning

The Johnson Murder Trial-A Boy's Leg Crushed.
Owingsville, June 13.—The preliminary examination of W. Anderson Johnson, charged with the murder of Isaac Alfney in the extreme eastern portion of tuis county, is in progress at this place, having been called yesterday before Hon. E. N. Brother. county judge, and is exciting the deepest interest, the court room being well filled all the time. The prosecution, represented by Col. J. S. Hust and Reuben Gudgell, county attorney, closed their testimony yesterday afternoon, and in it shut out all hope of the defendant to prove up a case of self-defense as he thought he would be able to prove without much trouble. The defense, represented by Hon. Henry L. Stone. of Mt. Sterling, Judge N. P. Reid, Hon. Van B. Young; C. W. Goodpaster and W. R. Patterson, a splendid array of legal talent. are making a desperate flight for an acquittal in this court, but they will certainly fail, and to-morrow when the case closes, Johnson will doubtless be held over on a moderate bail bond, which he is well able to give.

Bill Turner, a young colored boy about ten years of age, living in this city with his parents, had the upper portion of his right leg and thigh most horribly crushed and mangled yesterday evening, and the prospects are it will cost him his life. Yesterday evening as the freight wagon from Mt. Sterling was coming into town, Bill ran behind it, and swinging up, tried to steal a ride, but in some way his leg got caught in the wheel and was carried up between the wheel and bed and mashed fearfully. All the medical attention possible was rendered him, but he will in all probability die.

NEWS AND OTHER NOTINGS.
The Bedford Gazette wants an anti-cigarette law passed. Next?

Sebastian McKay, of Titusville, struck oil in his garden while digging for potatoes on Friday.

A wind and rain storm in Minnesota last Saturday and Sunday caused the loss of several lives and did considerable damage.

Three men were killed on Sunday by an explosion on the wrecking steamer B. & J. Baker off Cape Henry beach.

A. D. Robeson, a nephew of ex-Secretary Robeson, was killed by lightning on Sunday near Hunnewell, Kan.

Five persons living near Solomen City, Kan., were killed on Thursday by a cyclone, which also destroyed many buildings.

A stately woman walked solemnly down California street, San Francisco, dressed only in a night-gown. She was insane.

Mr. John Black, of Oliver township, Perry county, has a colt that is only two years and twenty-two days old that weighs 1,322.

Logs that escape from the boom at Williamsport are worth 25 cents a piece to the finder. One man made over $100 in this way on Thursday.

A hundred persons were killed and sixty injured by an earthquake which recently devastated a number of villages in the Pashalie of Van Armenia.

Jew boys are preferred to any others as office boys by numbers of Christians in New York. They are found to be exceptionally intelligent and trustworthy.

Charles Johnson, of Eau Claire, Wis., was killed in his doorway on Friday by Louis Carter, a married man, who had tried to elope with Mrs. Johnson.

Father Larocca, General of the Dominican Order for the entire world, accompanied by Lieutenant General Calberry, has arrived at New York from Europe.

Mrs. Harper, a colored woman, living in Rock Hill township, Bueks county, accidentally shot and killed her husband on Thursday while examining a gun.

An insane woman at Clinton, Ill., committed suicide recently in a most horrible manner. She saturated her clothing with kerosene and then set them on fire.

Daniel Moran and Henry Donsberger, two of the men who were scalded by the explosion at Pottsville on Saturday have died, and L. Blakenhorn is not expected to survive.

—Mr. Flanagan and Mr. McDermitt, of White Mills, were both drowned at Kimble on Saturday afternoon. They were in a row-boat on a pleasure trip going to Lackawaxen.

—A special from Little Rock, Ark., says that near Arkadelphia, on Saturday last, Pleasant Gray, aged thirteen, shot and killed a colored boy named Russell of about the same age.

—The oldest minister in the world is believed to be Rev. John F. Adams, of the New Hampshire Conference. Of the ninety-four years he has lived, sixty-nine have been spent in the ministry.

—John Smith, living in Plymouth township, Montgomery county, was attacked by highwaymen on Thursday, who shot him dangerously and then robbed him of clothing and $17 in money.

—Two Michigan girls in love with the same man induced him to go to Utah and marry them both. This is a slight improvement on the old method of shooting one and eloping with the other.

—A terrible boiler explosion occurred at Pottsville about noon on Friday, at Atkins Bros. Fishback rolling mill. Eight or ten men were badly scalded and of those it is thought three at least will die.

—The wife of an old colored man in the eastern part of Georgia recently presented him with the sixth pair of twins, the family having been previously endowed with two pairs of triplets—all flourishing.

—By the explosion of the boiler of the steamboat Hannah, at New Orleans, on Wednesday, of last week, one man was killed, and a number of others were fatally injured, five of whom have since died.

—On Tuesday night Cal. Emory, who murdered his wife, was taken from jail at Russellville, Ark., by a mob and hung. The Governor only a few weeks ago commuted his death sentence to imprisonment for twenty-one years.

—Michael Connally was killed, Patrick Burke seriously injured and John Hawkins had his leg broken on Monday at No. 2 mine of the Delaware and Hudson Coal Company, at Plymouth, Pa. The accident was caused by a premature blast.

—A chartor has been filed in Kansas for a co-operative society to colonize Old Mexico. It is for the purpose of buying lands in Mexico and settling colonies there on a capital stock of $200,000 divided into eight thousand shares of $25 each.

—Isaac Alfrey's dog bit Anderson Johnson's hog, at Owingsville, Ky. Then Johnson shot Alfrey's dog. Next, Alfrey shot Johnson's hog. Finally, Johnson shot Alfrey, killing him, and the latest report said that a mob had gone to hang the murderer.

A turkey gobble on the farm of W. C. Beates, of East Donegal township, Lancaster county, recently undertook to carry a full-grown chicken on its back. The chicken kept her balance nicely, and was carried for some time before the gobble tilted her off.

Diphtheria has become epidemic at Lerdington, Mich. One hundred and twenty children have died recently in a population of 4,000 people. The schools are closed, and special policemen have been stationed at the houses where sickness exists to prevent ingress and egress.

A man employed in an ice house in Wisconsin, Me., lost his footing and fell, involuntarily throwing his arms wildly in the air. His pick was thrown in such a manner that the back of his neck struck upon the sharp point, severing an artery, and he bled to death in five minutes.

George C. Gatling stabbed and killed his wife at the Atlantic Beer Gardens, San Francisco, on Thursday evening. He suspected her of infidelity and wrote her a decoy note, which she answered by going to the gardens. He met her in the room and stabbed her to the heart.

Reuben E. Brown, a farmer of Limestone township, four miles from Peoria, Ill., while crossing an iron bridge over the Kickapoo river in a wagon during a thunder storm on Saturday evening, was struck by lightning and instantly killed. His son, a lad of 12 years, who was with him, was not hurt.

One of the Protestant churches in Patchogue, L. I., has made a novel addition to its music by introducing into the church two dozen canary birds in cages. They sing with the choir and also when the choir is not singing, and their music is not complained of by either the minister or the congregation.

Dr. Harry Darling, of Atlanta, Ga., while visiting Niagara Falls week before last, was so smitten by the charms of a girl who sold relics in one of the museums—Anne Murphy, of St. Catharines,—that he proposed, was accepted and the next day they were married and started for the sunny South.

As a gang of men were at work on Saturday at Lafayette, Ind., tearing down the old Court House, preparatory to the erection of shares of $200,000 divided into eight thousand and shares of $25 each.
As a gang of men were at work on Saturday at Lafayette, Ind., tearing down the old Court House, preparatory to the erection of a new building, the roof fell in, burying four men. Three of these—William Hucy, Samuel Buckner and Peter Cook—received fatal injuries, while the fourth escaped with only slight bruises.

A terrible cyclone visited Wisconsin, a few miles south of Hopkins, on Sunday evening, causing a great destruction of property and killing James Young, whose wife was so badly hurt that she will probably die. John Crabill and several members of his family were also badly hurt, several of whom will likely die.

Father Maloney, the exposed miracle worker of Erie, who was arrested on a charge of obtaining money under false pretenses, was discharged on Tuesday. For the SENTINEL News From the Old Dominion State.
A friend writing from mouth of Wilson, Va., says:

"Pandemonium has suddenly broken loose hereabouts. Jerome Pasely, a young man who has been with me for some time, shot and killed a negro while endeavoring to arrest him for an attempted outrage on the person of a little girl nine years of age. The particulars are as follows: The negro came to Mr. Masten Halsey's where Pasely was at work, fired his pistol as he came into the yard, peremptorily ordered Mrs. Halsey to get his breakfast, and then went up stairs. Pasely summoned assistance, went up stairs and ordered him to surrender. His answer was a pistol shot fired point blank at Pasely's breast. The officer caught the ball in the fleshy part of the forearm, promptly knocked the negro down, while his assistants grappled with him, caught up a shot gun and fired the contents into his abdomen, making a ghastly wound from which his bowels and liver protruded. He was a spunky negro, fought desperately to the last, and met death with steal, voiceless indifference. The location of the tragedy is near here, on the Carolina line; the negro's name was McAllen, and he claimed to have come from Yadkin county.

A negro husband and wife who live in Ashe county, "Old North State," some seven miles away, had "a little tuff tother day." The woman (to use her own elegant diction) "just mopped cuten the lazy cuss with a piece of fence rail," and stabbed him in several places with a "case" knife. He fainted from loss of blood. No arrests.

Four prisoners broke jail at Independence, Va. a few days since. Among them was a negro sentenced to be hung in October for killing a couple of his brothers-in-law. Another man in the prison for deliberate murder refused to be liberated. The leader in the gang is a sharper, locks and bolts were little in his way. He stole a horse and crossed the mountain twenty miles away before day on the same night they escaped.

A little negro dwarf was hung in Helton township Asho county, not long since, for stabbing a white girl. A man by the name of Lynch performed this Tristran hanging work.

Three loads of Davie and Alexander county men passed through this village a few days since, making a mountain tour.

Crops are good; fine crops of tobacco that will find a market in Winston this winter. D. I.

Col. L. L. Polk, Secretary of the State Agricultural Society, makes the following announcement in the Raleigh News: I will establish on the fair grounds at Raleigh an office, in charge of a competent gentlemen, who will keep during the week of the fair, a register of all ex-soldiers in the city, together with such notes or information as they desire to be exchanged with each other. Each command will have its own register, and the members on arrival could report to the office, register their names and old commands, their present residence, etc. These registers will be open at all times for the information of the public. It would be a general intelligence office for all the ex-soldiers and their friends, where cards could be exchanged, messages deposited and delivered, appointments for meetings made, etc. Programmes for each day will be published and distributed gratuitously each morning, and in these the announcements of meetings would be published.

Commissioner Raum has decided that "Rock and Rye" is not a medicine, but a beverage, and taxable as such. That settles it. If Rock and Rye is not a medicine editors will no longer drink it. If any of them have formed an appetite for the stuff, which they find it difficult to overcome, they should try cod liver oil which is a medicine but not a beverage.

FREEDING THEM OUT OF THEIR OWN Spoon.—The prohibitionists hereabouts are getting all they asked for, if they did have their hind sights knocked off in the late election. They can't get whiskey except on a doctor's prescription! We have heard of two who applied at bars in this place since the election, who couldn't get it without a paper in due form. And "they say" it is the law as to them, and like the laws of the Medes and Persians, which change not. What will they do when a fellow gets snake bit and there is no doctor around?—Salesbury Watchman.

Gold mining was begun in North Carolina in the early part of this century, and up to 1827 she was the only gold producing State.

THE MURDER OF ROBERT
YONLEY.
Our readers are already acquainted with the fact of the murder of Mr. Robt. Yonley, formerly a resident of Pope county, and a brother to Mrs. G. W. Chapman, of our town. The murder, a most cruel one, was perpetrated at Red Bluff on the L. R. and Pine Bluff R. R., some thirty miles below Little Rock, on the 8th of August last, by three negroes named Whit Brown, Charles Scott and Ben Reynolds, who robbed Mr. Yonly of $250 in money.

It is with pleasure that we record the capture of the murderers by detective Sib Bayse, of Little Rock, who has been working up the case since its occurrence, assisted by constable Washmood. The Gazette says of Brown that he was known as a desperate character in Little Rock, and that he had gone hand in hand with crime in that city. The capture is thus described in the Gazette:

"When the two men arrived at Brown's door, Bayse remarked as he drew his revolver: 'Hold the lantern, I'll break in on him.' Throwing his weight against the door the old boards yielded, and Bayse sprang into the room, bounded to an old bed of straw, and as Brown attempted to rise, placed his pistol against him, saying, 'Lie down or I'll kill you. Here Wash, put the hand-cuffs on him.' Scott was in an adjoining room, but before he could rub his eyes sufficiently to see himself as others saw him, the muzzle of a pistol was placed against the top of his head also."

From Brown the whereabouts of Reynolds was obtained, and the officers wisely made quick work of his arrest also. So that all three of the villians were nicely taken in, and are now in custody where they await the stern demands of justice.

A private letter to Col.G.W. Chapman, from Woodson, last week stated that intelligence had been recei-

ved at that place that the citizens around Red Bluff had taken the law into their own hands, and had lynched one of the negroes. We have not, however, seen anything in the papers to that effect, and suppose that it was a mistaken rumorange in the papers to that effect, and suppose that it was a mistaken rumor which sprang as a kind of spontanuity from the excited state of feeling over the atrocious crime.

Since writing the above we learn that the hanging was done to make Brown reveal the particulars of the murder and the parties interested in it, and was only done to obtain this information.

This morning the attendance was very slim and there is a growing feeling that the dropping out of the leading contestants was due mainly to the fact the gate money, and consequently the profits, both to walkers and managers, is likely to be small. Hart and Hughes, it is said, will be brought forward at no distant day in a match with Rowell and others, if possible, as the last chance of exciting public interest and making the exhibitions pay. Where the Shoe Pinches.

NEW YORK, March 2.—Speaking of the French edict against American meats, the Commercial Bulletin says:

It is charged, and not denied, that since the export trade in meats has been done direct from the western packers, to the European dealers, without insignificance and overreaction at the seaboard, all this complaint of trichina has been heard.

There appears to be but one remedy, and that lies in the enforcement of official inspection at New York, and in the refusal of the European importers to accept any goods that have not been so inspected.

Hospital for Intemperate Women.

HARTFORD, CONN., March 2.—The corporators of the Women's National hospital for the treatment of women addicted to the excessive use of alcohol or narcotics have chosen Dr. Marion Sims, of New York, president. The trustees are leading physicians from ten different States. Governor Bigelow and staff left to-night for Washington.

Local Option Defeated in Indiana.

INDIANAPOLIS, March 2.—The local option law was defeated in the senate to-day by a vote of 33 yeas to 25 nays. The time for the adjournment of the regular session by constitutional limitation will expire next Monday, but there is a large amount of business on the files that cannot be reached by that time, and it is probable that an extra session will be called immediately on the adjournment of the regular session.

A Deplorable State of Affairs in Honolulu.

SAN FRANCISCO, March 2.—The Bulletin this afternoon will publish an interview with a reliable gentleman passenger by the bark-

entine Ella, which arrived here yesterday from Honolulu. He reports a deplorable condition of affairs there. The small-pox is epidemic, many houses are quarantined, no one is allowed to enter or leave the city and intercommunication between the islands has been stopped. The city is in a very bad sanitary condition, not a single sewer within its limits and the ground is honeycombed with vaults, which have not been cleaned in a quarter of a century.

BORDENTOWN, N. J., March 2.—George W. English, city collector, who killed himself a year ago was, found to have been a defaulter for a considerable amount.

COLUMBUS, O., March 2.—The governor to-day commuted the sentence of John Welsh, who was to have been hung for murder at Fremont next Friday, to imprisonment for life.

COLUMBUS, O., March 1.—Governor Foster to-day granted a pardon to Ferdinand Seitz, of Hamilton county, who was received on a life sentence for murder thirty years ago and has spent that length of time in prison.

GALVESTON, March 2.—Last night as the Monus procession was passing the English kitchen two shots rang out and Mrs. Elizabeth Perceviel, the proprietress, fell mortally wounded by her divorced husband, Richard Stevens.

Progress of the Whittaker Case.
NEW YORK, March 2.—In the Whittaker case the letter of warning and other communications were admitted, but as specimens of handwriting only. The letters were given to William E. Hogan, of Troy, expert, who will examine and report the result on Monday next, till which time the court adjourned.

A Band of Young Villains.

NEW YORK, March 2.—A band of young robbers were captured to-day, the oldest ten and the youngest seven years of age. The boys banded together for the purpose of robbing children going to and from school, and had made a number of successful assaults, dividing the plunder, consisting of slates, books, jack-knives and odd pennies.

Another Murder Near Springfield.

NASHVILLE, March 2.—The American's Springfield special reports the killing last night of Sam Gaines, colored, near the Kentucky line. He was called out by a party of masked men, supposed to be from Kentucky. The body was found fifty yards from his door this morning, full of bullet-holes. The men are supposed to be friends of the person with whom Gaines had a difficulty a year ago.

End of a Wild Young Man.

St. Louis, March 2.—Charles Wilde, a young man who has been doing a grain brokerage business on change for a year past, was arrested to-day under an indictment charging him with obtaining money under false pretenses. It is alleged that he has been in the habit of purchasing grain from commission merchants for shipment to Baltimore and other places, and hypothecating the bills of lading, raising in this way some twelve or more thousand dollars, which he has lavished on fast women and lost speculating at bucket-shops.

Shot by an Officer.

Shot by an Officer.

SEDALLA, Mo., March 2.—A negro named Burnett was shot and killed by City-Marshal Telhart, at Lamonte, ten miles west of here, last night. Burnett went home drunk, beat his mistress, and drove her from the house. She took refuge at a neighbor's named Chaffay. Burnett followed her with a club, and was met by Chaffay, who forbade him to enter his yard. At this juncture Marshal Telhart appeared on the scene and commanded Burnett to surrender. He refused to be arrested, and advanced on Telhart with his club. The marshal again ordered him to surrender, but the negro still advanced in a menacing manner, when Telhart shot him. The coroner's justified the act of the marshal.

More of the Texas Land Frauds.

DALLAS. March 1.—A new link in the

More of the Texas Land Frauds.

DALLAS, March 1.—A new link in the great land frauds perpetrated in this State two or three years ago has just come to light here. A large basket of papers was found yesterday in the back yard of a proprietor of a house of ill fame, which proved by deeds to the lands of Wm. Bray or T. E. Tullis, with claims of titles including patents to lands in nearly every county of Texas and a number of powers of attorney from Tullis to Bray. There are also deeds to lands in Indiana and Tennessee, the whole amounting to 500,000 acres, also a number of letters written on printed letter-heads reading: "Texas and Indiana Mutual Exchange Colonization Bureau, Austin and Indianapolis, W. S. Webb, president, Wm. Berry, Secretary." Who Webb or Bray are, is not known, their names not being mentioned when the frauds were discovered two years ago, and Tullis, Hamm and others tried and sent to the penitentiary. The name of J. W. Bradley, of Boston, also figures in these papers and several deeds are made out to him from Bray. It is not known how or by whom the papers were placed where found, but it is believed that the finding of them will lead to the arrest of persons engaged in another big land swindle.

THE ALLEN MURDER TRIAL.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

GENEVA, Ill., March 2.—The Allen murder trial is again running under a full head of steam. The court-room to-day, as on former occasions, has been filled full of spectators from all the country around about here. The Triune representative had a pleasant little visit with the prisoners. Woodruff and Thomas, in their quarters in durance vile, in which they said they were confident of being discharged as soon as the trial is over. They seem to take things in a cool sort of manner, and say that, so far, they have not been scared. The trial will consume some little time over into next week, as two days have been nearly lost this week by the non-arrival of the Judge Monday. The interest down at Sandwich, where the murder was committed, in the trial is great, and all reports of its progress are looked for with great eagerness. Mrs. Mary Nichol, a servant, was put on the stand. She swore she had lived in the Allen family. Mrs. Allen, Libbile, and Mrs. Rood came home; was at the house the night of the murder; went to bed about 9 p.m.; heard Mrs. Rood leave the house; witness slept up-stairs; was not well that night; did not sleep well; heard a person walk lightly in the hallway; the door was open to the head of the stairs a little; heard a pistol go off; seemed as if it was out in the yard; heard it go off again; was excited; went down-stairs after a while; Mrs. Allen was in the sitting-room; pleasant and bright night, and frost on the ground; found Mr. Allen on the floor; did not see him lifted up; Libbile gave the alarm on the street; Mrs. Allen was frightened; stalled after the murder four days. On cross-examination she said she lived there in all about two months; did not hear any one speak in the hall; room door partially open; heard no shout-
animation she said she lived there in all about two months; did not hear any one speak in the hall; room door partially open; heard no shouting; was not present when the candle was found, but saw it in Mrs. Marks' hands; heard six shots fired; heard no talking in the hall.

Thomas H. Whipple was next sworn. He lived formerly in St. Charles; lived the great portion of twenty-six years in Chicago; am with Turtle's detective agency, Chicago; have been to Allen's house; procured the door-key while there once; gave it to Dr. Piper, of Chicago; there were marks on the storm of the key at the time; it was the key to the front door; key-hole was moderately large and the key turned easily. Cross-examined: Looked at the key with a magnifying glass; key was got from the floor of Allen's house; had the key for a few days, and then gave it to Piper.

J. Theo. Walker, sworn: Lived in Sandwich twenty-five years; was before the inquest; am a matchlist; knew Allen and his family; known Woodruff about eight years and Thomas fifteen years; quite well acquainted with Thomas; Thomas went to work for the Company about three weeks after the murder; saw him each morning; had a conversation with him about the murder; Thomas spoke about going to Leadville; witness told him about a man at the hotel who was sick, who was going to Leadville; Thomas said he did not care to have anything to do with him, as he was a detective; Thomas thought the man was looking up the Allen murder. On cross-examination: Knew a man named Peterman, a ditcher; this conversation was about three months after the murder; know about detectives being in the town; one was called Mirdock.

James Fitzgerald, the sick detective, was next called. Lived in Chicago for about eight years; heard about the Allen murder; was sent out by Turtle's agency about the 22d of April to Sandwich to look the ground over and report; stopped at the Sandwich House when he got there; looked the town over; saw Thomas on that day and on two days following; after this Thomas kept away from him; one night Thomas said, "There he goes"; was tracked by Thomas one night; Thomas was excited and changed in appearance when the witness was near; Thomas was at work in his yard one day and ran into the house as the witness approached; saw Thomas at the ivory stable one evening.

Cross-examined: Worked for Turtle's agency since 72 by the month; got into Sandwich April 22; read the testimony taken before the Coroner's jury; said he had been in Denver when he put up at the hotel; before being a detective was in the boot and shoe business in Massachusetts; did not get an introduction to Thomas; told Walker he might send Thomas around and he would tell him about Colorado; wanted to get into conversation with Thomas; Thomas followed him after the first three days he was in Sandwich; never before was in Sandwich; Thomas was walking with friends one evening when he said, "There he goes"; when he was excited was pale in the face and nervous; lips would move and his eyes would roun from one side to the other; never saw Thomas before the 22d; the first three days Thomas seemed natural; when he saw Thomas in the yard he was spading; when he met Thomas by the stable it was in the evening and getting dark; lights in the barn, but none anywhere else; the stable was cast of the depot; was light enough to see to read.

Miss Lilible Allen, the daughter, was next sworn, and took the stand: Have lived in Sandwich nine years; know Thomas and Woodruff; was at home on the night of the murder; were four in the family at the time; Mrs. Rood was in during the evening; father came home about 9 p.m. and locked the front door (key was shown her and recognized); Mrs. Rood wont away soon after; witness lot her out; house fronts Main stair; locked the door after Mrs. Rood went out; lock works easily, and the key fits the lock loosely; fathor retired before Mrs. Rood had left; after Mrs. Rood's departure went into the sitting-room to read; father and mother had gone to their room; did not read long, as fathor asked if it was not time to go to bed, and she wont; was awakened as if some one was pounding the floor; heard screams, and started down-stairs; saw a man come from the back parlor as she was on the stairs. He said: "Why don't you come on if you have got him?" She said: "Oh, Mr. Smith, what is the matter?" The person looked up at her and passed out. The first man that went out had an overcoat on and wore a cap. She was exceedingly frightened. The second man was larger and square-shouldered; was smooth-faced, she thought; went down-stairs and found her father on the floor. At this moment the witness went. Went to Smith.
man was larger and square-shouldered; was smooth-faced, she thought; went down-stairs and found her father on the floor. At this juncture the witness wept. Went to Smith's and gave the alarm; saw Thomas at the jail in Sycamoro. The witness was put in a bedroom and the prisoners of the jail were brought in and conversed with. When Thomas-spoke she recognized the voice as the one heard on the night of the murder. She fainted partially away. The questions asked were of great number. On the cross-examination the whole ground was traversed again without much change. The Court then adjourned for dinner.

With the discharge of this witness, Miss Allen, the prosecution rested their case. This early termination on the side of the people was quite a surprise. The first witness put on by the defense was Charles Hoadle, of Sandwich, who was the first man at Allen's house after the murder. His story was about the same as that of the witnesses put on by the people at the first of the trial.

At a farm-house about three miles from Bloomington, Ill., Will Lowery, while cleaning a revolver which he believed to be empty, pointed it at his sister Mary, and fired it. She fell, mortally wounded, and he was only by the utmost vigilance prevented from taking his own life.

The New York police have broke up an organized band of boy bandits in that city. The oldest was 10 and the youngest 7. They had conspired to rob children on their way to and from school. A large collection of books, slates, pencils, etc., was found at their headquarters.

John Hunter, who was recently elected receiver of taxes at Philadelphia, has given testimony before an investigating committee to show that the gas-consuming public of that city is being defrauded to the amount of $1,000 per day by the gas trus.

Henry Hill, a negro, who murdered the jailer at Hartwell, Ga., was caught in the woods, while roasting a potato at a fire. At last advices three hundred people was hovering around the jail, threatening to lynch the butcher.

A brutal murder was committed in Gallatin county, Ky. One O'Neal attacked a neighbor named Andrew Gibner with an ax, cut his head to pieces, and then cut off one arm. He was arrested at his house.

Burglars entered the residence of E. P. Smith, at the corner of Wabash avenue and Twenty-fourth street, Chicago, chloro-formed the people of the house, and carried off $2,000 in cash and a $500 diamond.

The brothers Boca, who murdered an editor named Conkling at Socorro, New Mexico, have been caught in Texas, and are being brought back by rangers. It is believed that they will be lynched.

Vigilantes at Albuquerque, New Mexico, took from jail and hanged to a tree Faustine Gulittero, implicated in the murder of Colonel Potter. This is the fourth lynching for participation in this crime.

A series of systematic robberies has been discovered in the National Bank of Virginia, at Richmond. By a system of false entries the bookkeeper having charge of individual accounts stole $23,000.

Charles Merrill, of China, Me., killed his mother in a barn, concealed her body in the hay until frozen, then cut it into pieces, part of which he burned, burying the remainder in the snow.

Frederick W. Davies, a young Welchman of high culture, was whipped on the bare back at Richmond, Va., under sentence of the police court, for stealing clothing.

Thos. Smith, who forced his son to walk in a recent pedestrian contest in New York, has been fined $100 and sent to prison for ten days for cruelty to his child.

A negro named Burnett was killed at Lamonte, Mo., the other might by the city marshal. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable murder.

A deficiency of $85,000 has beed discovered in the accounts of the Springfild, Mass., Silk company. Henry Hallett, the treasurer, has the most of it.

Henry Redding, collector of the St. Louis Elevator company, has been arrested for the embezzlement of $2,000, which he lost in bucket-shops.

An eighteen years old boy in the Foxboro, Mass., alms house, Samuel Furner by name, has been arrested for raping Sarah Adams, aged 46.

Jordan Thomas, a mulatto barber, has eloped from Lancaster, O., with Lucretia Watts, said to be a very handsome white girl.

In the trial of Colonel Cash, the South Carolina duelist, for the murder of William Shannon, the jury failed to agree.

The superintendent of schools at Little Rock, Ark., reports that many pupils carry loaded pistols and dangerous knives.

Thomas Skelton, the jailer at Hartwell, Ark., was murdered by the only prisoner in his charge, Henry Hill, a negro.

Safe blowers robbed the postoffice at Wayland, Mich., of $1,500 in money and stamps.

A Brutal Negro Done For.
Sedalia, Mo., March 4.—News was received in this city this morning of a tragedy which occurred at Lamonte, ten miles west of Sedalia, on Tuesday evening, at 6 o'clock. Ben Burnett, a negro, got drunk and went home with a big jug of hard cider. He lives with a negro mistress, having driven his lawful wife off last spring. His paramour, seeing that he had already taken too much, poured the contents of the jug out. When Ben found this out he was in a terrible rage, and got a gun to shoot his mistress. She fled for protection to the house of a white man named Chaffey. Ben followed her, entered Chaffey's house, picked up a stone crock, struck the woman in the head with it and knocked her down. He then went home. The woman went in search of an officer, and then returned to the house where Ben was. He took up a large club when he saw her, threatening to kill her, and a second time drove her to Chaffey's house for protection. The first time Chaffey was not at home. The second time he was. When he saw Ben coming after the woman Chaffey warned the enraged negro not to enter his premises. Ben struck at Chaffey several times and swore he would come in. At this moment Philip Zilhart, city marshal, appeared on the scene. He called on Burnett to surrender. The negro cursed him, swore that he would not be taken, and at the same time advanced on the marshal with his club. Zilhart warned him to stop, but the negro still advanced. Zilhart fired on him. The negro continued to approach, and Zilhart snapped his pistol at him several times. Suddenly Burnett sank to the ground, and died in a few minutes. Coroner King examined the case to-day. The verdict of the jury war: "Killed in self-defense."

Resignation of J. W. Simonton of the Associated Press.
NEW YORK. July 27.—J. W. Simonton
Resignation of J. W. Simonton of the Associated Press.
New York, July 27.—J. W. Simonton, General Agent of the New York Associated Press, some time since tendered his resignation owing to ill health and pressure of private interests. The association endeavored to induce him to retain his position. Mr. Simonton however insisted upon the acceptance of his resignation to take place not later than the 1st of October in order to devote himself to his private interests and especially to recover his health impaired by too close attention to office duties. At a meeting of the executive committee of the New York Associated Press today the following expression of opinion of the association in regard to the voluntary retirement of J. W. Simonton as general agent was adopted:

That Mr. Simonton has been general agent of the association since November 5, 1866, and that in all these years he has discharged the duties of his responsible and arduous work with great fidelity to the several members of the association, and with general acceptance to the public.

The office is one which requires capacity, integrity, and industry, and we have never found the general agent wanting in any of these qualities. Mr. S. leaves the association of his own free will, and not at the request or wish of any of its members. In accepting his resignation, our best wishes go with him, for his complete restoration to health, and for personal happiness and prosperity in all the future of his life.

Mr. J. C. Huston, at present Associated Press agent in London, has been chosen as Mr. Simonton's successor.

The Coles Shooting.

At the inquest to-day, in the case of George Coles, shot in the Bowery by Mrs. Coleman, the jury returned a verdict, accusing her of the crime. The woman returned no answer to the question as to what she had to say, and was committed to the Tombs to await the action of the grand jury.

FOURTH EDITION
THE FAITHLESS GUIDE.
Why Parker is said to have As-saulted Mrs. Bull.
WATERTOWN, N. Y., August 2.—Charles Parker, the North Woods guide, who so brutally assaulted Mrs. Buli, of Philadelphia, has been locked up in the Essex County Jail, in Elizabethtown. Parker lived in Elizabethtown, and was not a regular guide.

His reputation is not good, and it is said that he forged the name of Edward Butler, of Olmsteadville, last spring. He was not recognized by the old guides of the woods as a professional, and he acted chiefly for people who wanted a cheap guide. He was angry at this lack of recognition and threatened that if he was not used better he would spoil the guiding business in the Adirondacks. Some think the outrage was deliberately planned for this purpose, hence the wrath of the guides, who were out to the number of one hundred scouring the woods to find him after his flight.

They were all armed and would have shot him at sight. It is asserted that Parker's employer at the Forked Lake House tried to discourage pursuit of the villain. Parker is a bold, bad man. Mrs. Bull, after the assault had been made (the criminal almost choking her to death during her resistance), calmly looked the villain in the eye while they were crossing the lake and said to him: "You know you have committed a horrible crime and you know that you will suffer for it." The fiend at once replied that if she thought so the better way would be to end the affair at once by drowning her. "I can do it," said he, "anywhere in this lake and nobody will ever know anything about this." His actions indicated that he was about to carry his murderous threat into execution when the lady with great presence of mind quieted him by replying that she hoped he would say nothing about the affair to anyone. The brute thereupon ceased his threats. As soon as the bomb landed, Mrs. Bull rushed into the cottage of Senator Plant's wife and revealed the truth. What followed has already been narrated.

A GUIDE'S CRIME.
The Outrageous Assault on a Lady by an Adirondack Guide.
The Albany Argus has the following particulars of the dastardly assault by the North Woods guide upon the person of Mrs. Geo. Bull:

"W. F. Hall, of New York city, who, with his wife, arrived at Chester Wednesday night, gives some account of the outrage committed upon the person of Mrs. Bull, at what is called Butternilk Carry, between Forked and Long Lakes, last Tuesday. Mr. and Mrs. Hall first made the acquaintance of Mrs. Bull at the North River Hotel, while she was en route for ex-Senator Platt's camp at Long Lake.

"They accompanied her to Blue Mountain Lake. Upon their arrival there they found that Mrs. Bull's trunk had been left behind; they all waited over one day for the missing trunk, and as it did not arrive, Mr. and Mrs. Hall proceeded on their journey, leaving Mrs. Bull to follow next day, Tuesday. Mrs. Bull, accompanied by Chas. Parker, who had been recommended as a safe, reliable man, as her guide, proceeded on her way to the camp of ex-Senator Platt.

It was while crossing the last carry between Forked Lake and Long Lake that the heinous crime was committed. While crossing the lake after leaving the carry the villain extorted a promise of silence from the lady under threats of drowning. Upon arriving at the camp she was met on the shore by her friends. Mr. Hall states that the ladies of the party already in camp, not having been so promptly apprised of the coming of Mrs. Bull, were behind Mr. Hall in reaching the shore of the lake where the guide was landing. Upon reaching the shore Mr. Hall at once saw there was some trouble from the appearance of the lady, who, upon stepping ashore and seeing her friends, had an attack of hysteria.

"As the guide attempted to push off his boat, Mr. Hall seized it by the bow and ordered Parker to keep quiet. He then called for the guides of ex-Senator Platt to come to his assistance. None of them at this time really knew what the trouble was. Mrs. Platt and Mrs. Hall were in the meantime endeavoring to restore Mrs. Bull to consciousness, while Mr. Hall and the Senator ordered the other guides, three in number, at the camp, to detain Parker until the matter could be investigated. During the confusion, however, Parker jumped ashore and escaped into the woods. The alarm was promptly spread, but owing to the limited number of available men, and the distance from the different avenues of escape, Parker reached his own camp, secured his rifle, and had about two hours start of his pursuers. Mr. and Mrs. Hall came away sooner than they expected, for the purpose of aiding in putting men on the track of Parker.

"Mrs. Bull still remains at ex-Senator Platt's camp. A dispatch from Kingston, Ont., says a man supposed to be Parker was arrested there Thursday."

Guide Parker Shot While Escaping. Thor, Aug. 9. — Charles Parker, the Adirondack guide who committed a heinous assault on Mrs. Bull, of Philadelphia, and who escaped from the officer in Blue Mountain Lake on Tuesday last, was caught early this morning by Officer Cole near Ausable Lake, after a desperate encounter, in which Parker received a probably mortal wound. charles-parker-1881-07.A16:
Mrs. Bull's Assailant—Capture of Parker, the Flend Guide—He is Shot While Attempting to Escape.

ALBANY, Aug. 10.—A brief dispatch Monday announced that Charles Parker, the North woods guide charged with a criminal assault upon Mrs. Bull, had been arrested at Long Lake and shot by Constable Cole, from whose custody he had escaped Tuesday night.

The particulars of this last phase of the affair are as follows: After his escape Parker hid in the woods. Constable Cole made search for him and at 11 o'clock Friday morning an interview was arranged at the foot of Long Lake to take place between Cole and Parker, the constable promising, as alleged, not to arrest the latter. Parker came to the place of meeting at the head of the outlet, accompanied by his wife, Cole and his deputy being on the opposite bank. After some conversation Parker, who had advanced into the center of the river, began to pull back to the shore. Cole called to him ordering him to surrender or he would shoot. Parker increased the speed of his boat and brought it around so that the person of his wife came between him and the constable. As the boat struck shore Parker jumped out, and as he was reaching down in the boat for his gun, Cole fired one shot at him from the Winchester rifle he carried. Parker immediately fell back on the rocks, moaning piteously, and his wife leaping from the boat, it went floating down the stream. Kelley, Cole's deputy, removed his shoes, and swimming over to the boat, got into it, and going over to the other side took the constable in, and crossing over again captured Parker. It was then ascertained that the shot from Cole's rifle had taken effect in Parker's left arm, about an inch below the shoulder, badly shattering the bone and completely disabling him. After striking his arm it entered his breast near the nipple and took a downward course. Dr. Woodward, who is summering at Raquette Lake, attended the wounded man and states that Parker has but a bare possibility of recovery. Great indignation prevails among the people, and threats against Cole are heard on every hand. It would not be a safe matter for him to show himself at the Forked Lake House, if the guides collected there mean all they say.
charles-parker-1881-07.A18:
Parker, the Guide, Dead.
Some Queer Reports in Circulation.
Parker, the Adirondack guide who was charged with an assault upon a lady relative of Senator Platt, of Connecticut, and who was shot after his escape from custody by Constable Cole at Long Lake, died at Forked Lake Tuesday morning, after having given his ante-mortem statement. It is alleged that Parker was cornered by the constable and shot because he would not submit, and that he remained lying where he was shot for thirty hours before Dr. Martine arrived to attend him, and that when found he was without covering or care, and would allow no one to move him. Dr. Martine had a stretcher made, had him put on it and rowed to the Forked Lake House, five miles away. The ball entered the region of the stomach and cannot be found. Dr. Martine says he never saw a more pitifiable sight nor a greater sufferer than Parker. Parties from the Adirondacks say there are two sides to the main story, and that sympathy is about equally divided. The impression obtains that it was intended Parker should escape when he did, and that Cole made an annoying blunder in attempting to rearrest him. A person just returned from the north woods says the feeling in favor of Parker is confined to a small number of the less reputable portion of the Adirondack community, and that the better class unanimously condemned him and denounced his crime. Parker's friends declared, on the day of the shooting, that he would give himself up upon certain conditions, and a message was sent to Senator Platt to that effect. The shooting and capture occurred before the message was received, but the fact that it was sent seems to give color to the report that there was a truce, for a time, and some negotiations between the officer and Parker, previous to his capture, out of which the story now current in Parker's favor may have been manufactured. It is currently reported that Parker had said he would not be taken alive, and that Warren Cole could never take him, and the officer was undoubtedly prepared for a desperate resistance, and for desperate measures. — Troy Times, August 10.

CINCINNATI, November 22. A. Garrett
HOW THE VICTIM WAS BETRAYED INTO A CONFESSION.
CINCINNATI, November 22.—A Gazette special from Athens, Ohio, states that when Davis, who was lynched at that place Sunday night, was taken to the bridge with a rope around his neck, he was asked to confess. He inquired what would be done with him if he confessed. They told him he would be taken back to jail to be dealt with by law. Being assured they would not hang him if he confessed, he said "I'm the man." At this there was an instant cry, "Throw him off." The other end of the rope was made fast to the bridge. They gave him three minutes in which to pray, but he did not attempt a prayer. He said he was ready to die, and when the time expired he was hurried off the bridge and his neck was broken by the fall.

A Negro Lynched at Albany, O.
ATHENS, O., Nov. 21.—Chris Davis, a mulatto, who was in jail for an outrageous assault upon an elderly woman, Mrs. Locke, living at Albany, O., was hanged by a mob last night. The Sheriff was overpowered and held while the mob broke into the cell and took Davis out. This morning his dead body was found hanging to a bridge over the Hocking River at the south edge of town. The mob was not masked, and will be arrested.

When Davis was taken to the bridge with the rope around his neck, he was asked to confess. He inquired what would be done with him if he confessed. They told him he would be taken back to jail to be dealt with by law. He hesitated, and again asked if they would not hang him if he confessed. Being a second time assured that they would not, he said: "I'm the man." At this there was an instant cry of "Throw him off!" The other end of the rope was made fast to the bridge. They gave him three minutes in which to pray, but he did not attempt a prayer. He said he was ready to die. When the time expired he was buried off the bridge, and his neck was broken by the fall. The Coroner held an inquest, but has not given a verdict.

CHRIS. DAVIS, the mulatto who committed a rape upon an old lady named Luekey, living at Albany, Athens county, about three weeks ago, was taken from the jail at Athens about 2 o'clock on Monday morning, and conveyed to the bridge across the Hocking river, when a rope was put around his neck and the other end tied to the bridge and he was pushed off, falling a distance of nine feet, breaking his neck. The mob consisted of thirty or forty persons, and came from the neighborhood where the crime was committed. They gained admission to the jail on pretense of delivering a horse thief. The sheriff, who admitted the party, was seized and held until the victim was secured. The houses of the town officials and all the churches were guarded, so that no alarm could be given. As soon as the hanging was over the mob scattered in all directions, and if it is not positively known who were implicated, the body of Davis was found early in the morning dangling from the bridge.

Law or License?
There is a lawless spirit abroad that bodes evil unless it shall be promptly arrested by a vigorous revival of a healthy public sentiment. While good citizens in Washington are avowing sympathy with an attempt at deliberate murder, equally respected citizens of other localities, in almost every section of the Union, are becoming actual murderers by seizing and unlawfully putting to death persons suspected or believed to have committed crimes for which the penalty is execution.

Within the last ten days a number of the oldest and best ordered of the Northwestern States have been disgraced by lawchings, and some of these have occurred under circumstances calculated to destroy all respect for law and the appliances of justice. As an illustration of this take the case of Ed. Williams, of Wisconsin, one of the alleged murderers of the Colman brothers. A telegram of the 19th instant says:

Williams was caught in Hall County, Nebraska, last Saturday and conveyed to Durand, where he arrived yesterday. In court this afternoon he pleaded not guilty to the charge of murder. The court-room was crowded and several men were outside. Williams had scarcely entered his plea and asked for time to procure witnesses when a noose was thrown over his neck. Those inside the court-room shoved him to a window, while those outside pulled the rope, and he was dragged some forty rods to a tree and hanged until he was dead.

There is no excuse, no possible palliation of such outlawry. If organized society is better than anarchy, if law is better than license, if there is to be any respect for the rights of person and property, if we are not to plunge into chaos, such proceedings as that murder at Durand must be stopped. The alleged outlaw was sure of a fair trial if the mob had spared him, and he would undoubtedly have been lawfully hanged in due course of time and justice.

A MOB'S VENGEANCE.
Negro Lynched at Athens for a Horrible Crime.
ATHENS, O., November 21.—Chris. Davis, a mulatto, in jail here for raping and assaulting with intent to kill Lucinda Luckey, at Albany in this county, recently, was last night taken from the jail and banged by a mob. The Sheriff was overpowered and held while the jail was broken open. Davis was in a cell, but the other prisoners were compelled to point him out, and the cell was broken open with a sledge. He was this morning found hanging on the South bridge. The mob was not masked, and the parties will be arrested. At the time of the outrage, when Davis was arrested, there were threats of lynching, and the prisoner was removed to Chillicothe for safety. Recently he was returned to the jail in this city.

The story of Davis's crime is as follows: The scoundrel had been living on and tending the farm belonging to Mrs. Luckey for some years. It appears that the black came to the widow Luckey's house on Saturday evening. November 5, at about 8 o'clock (she being alone), and made villainous proposals to her. She being afraid of him, coaxed him, and finally persuaded him to leave. She then barred the door and made it as secure as possible.

At about 2 in the morning she was awakened by the unceremonious entrance of the negro by smashing the door and frame down. She attempted to get up and run, but he caught her by the throat and jerked her down on the floor with such force that her senses left her. When she became conscious she got up and, with much difficulty, walked to a neighbor's, but could not tell her story until late Sunday.

In the meantime the negro went to Sabbath school and delivered a long prayer. But he was sent for, and came in the evening, much against his will. There was strong talk of lynching him at the time, but the big 200 pounder was lodged safely in jail.

The Cowan Affair.
One of the best citizens of the Cowan district gives us the following particulars in regard to the late row in Cowan : The affair originated in the store of Pattie & Shook, between a Mr. Northcutt, an employe of the Tennessee Coal & Railroad Company, and two negroes from the furnace, in which Northcutt got the best of it. The negroes threatened to have revenge. About thirty of them gathered at the saw mill with avowed intentions to mob Northcutt, but some of his friends had telegraphed him at Tracy to prepare himself to meet them. Thus warned, Northcutt and the other hands on his train armed the other hands on his train,) saw the negroes in waiting, and jumped on the train and advanced upon them, firing several shots, without aiming to hurt them, whereupon the negroes fled. to the furnace grounds. This ended the affair.

SEIZURE OF ILICIT DISTILLERIES.

WASHINGTON, March 17.—General Rauza, Commissioner of Internal Revenue, has received a report from Floyd Courthouse, Va., giving in detail an account of a recent raid upon illicit distilleries in that portion of the State. The raid occupied several days, and resulted in the capture and destruction of a number of distilleries. Among those destroyed was the large establishment situated on Runnel Bog creek, Franklin county, run by Dave Gillespie. John Lawson's distillery, situated near the bend of the Dan river, was seized and destroyed. State Brothers' large distillery, near the Pinnacles, was seized and the proprietors arrested and sent to jail in Patrick county. An establishment known as Souler's, near the North Carolina line, was destroyed. At last accounts the locality was infested with armed squads of illicit distillers lying in wait for the internal-revenue officers. The latter are well provided with arms, and are prepared for emergencies.

WASHINGTON, March 47.—Senator Edmuns left Washington last night for a visit to Florida. Senator Vance, of North Carolina, has paired with him for the remainder of the session. Judge Edmuns for some time has been troubled with a bad cold, and now seeks a warm climate in order to avoid the threatened danger of its developing into bronchitis or possibly settling on his lungs.

LAWLESSNESS IN VIRGINIA.
HOOES WHIRRED BOOERED DRIVEN
NEGROES WHIPPED, ROBEED AND DRIVEN FROM THEIR HOMES—OFFICERS OF JUSTICE INDIFFERENT.

WASHINGTON, May 3.—Internal Revenue Agent Tracie, who has been conducting the raids upon the illicit distillers in Franklin County, Va., has forwarded to Commissioner Raum a detailed account of a recent attempt to capture the notorious Dave Gillespie, which failed, the offender escaping from his house. The report says:

Since my raid in Running Bog on the 20th, Gillespie and his crowd of supporters (violators of the revenue laws) have committed shameful outrages upon innocent colored people in that neighborhood, whom they charged with giving information to the Revenue officers. They went in disguise, with their faces blackened, and whipped men and women, robbed one or two of money, destroyed their property, drove them from their homes, some of them half naked, and formed thirteen of them into one party on the road to West Virginia and ordered them to leave, on penalty of death if they returned.

These outrages have not disturbed in the slightest degree the officials of Franklin County. This revival of Ku-Kluxism by illicit distillers and their friends in the mountains of Franklin has terrorized good citizens to such an extent that they are afraid even to speak of the outrages, much less condemn them. There is no such thing in Franklin County, on the part of responsible citizens, as sympathy for the enforcement of the laws regarding making or selling spirits, either State or National.

When the United States Marshal's office has been stimulated to perform this part of their work I will have hopes of a better condition of affairs in Franklin County.

Conference on Military Matters—Other News.

WASHINGTON, May 3d.—General Sherman, General Sheridan and the Secretary of War had a long conference with the President today relative to the re-arrangement of military departments. Sheridan returns to Chicago to-morrow. It is believed that all the departments will be merged into departments East and West and will be commanded by Generals Sheridan and Hancock, with other Generals to be assigned to duty whenever more are available.

Additional articles of agreement have been concluded between the United States and Canada for the purpose of affording increased facilities for the exchange of letter correspondence and also for preventing the evasion by publishers of the postal laws and regulations of the United States.

Six per cent. bonds were received at the Treasury Department to-day for conversion into 3½ per cents, amounting to $7,868,256; total to date $60,690,150.

Boom Collapsed.

WICHITA, Kansas, May 3d.—The Oklahoma boom collapsed to-day on the receipt of the news of the unfavorable termination of the Paynes trial.

The President's Views.

WASHINGTON, May 3.—A reporter of the Western Associated Press visited the White House to-night and obtained the following version of the President's letter to Senator Dawes. The President did not retain a copy, but the note was short: In the first place, the President wrote that he was in favor of a free ballot and a fair count not only in Virginia, but in every State, and would encourage it, but he would not assist in elevating a man who, as the editor of a daily paper, is constantly attacking and defaming him and his administration. This referred to Gorham, editor of the National Republican and nominee of the Republicans for Secretary of the Senate. The above is substantially all that the letter to Dawes contained. In it the President said nothing about the pending nominations in the Senate. On this subject, however, the President maintained the same position he took before the caucus committee. He says he sent all the nominations to the Senate in good faith and that if the Senate sees fit to pass some of the nominations over, that is the business of the Senate, but the President cannot countenance any movement or suggestion for selecting certain nominations for consideration and leaving others unacted upon. As to what the Senate shall do, he has nothing to say or suggest; that is for the Senate to determine.

The President has been invited to accompany the Yorktown centennial company to visit the site of the battle of Yorktown on the steamer Despatch, on next Thursday.
