The mayor, of Elgin, Ill., and Alderman Jencks, Chairman of the Committee on Streets, have been censured by the Coroner's Jury for negligence in connection with the recent disaster on the Fox river.

Jay Cooke's country seat, Agontz, has been sold at Philadelphia for $113,-500.

The tow-boat John Parker, of the St. Louis and New Orleans line, has arrived at New Orleans with eight barges carrying 9,507 tons of grain.

President Garfield has withdrawn from the Senate the New York nominations for district attorneys and marshals, supposed to have been made in the interest of Senator Conkling.

A skull, believed to be that of Mrs. Lizzie Lowell, has been found near Lewiston, Me. A headless skeleton, identified as that of Mrs. Lowell, was found near the same spot seven years ago, and her husband, James Lowell, was convicted of murdering her. He is now in the State Prison for the crime.

The puddlers of the steel mill of the Reading, Pa., Iron Works, who struck a month ago for an advance in wages from $3.50 to $4.50 per ton, resumed work at the old figures. It is understood that an advance in the future has been promised.

The next reunion of soldiers takes place at Cincinnati, Ohio, September 15, 16 and 17.

By the fall of a building at Littleton, N. H., Wednesday, two women were killed and seven others were severely injured.

Henry Ward Beecher was served with a summons at Baltimore, in the suit of the Coroner's Jury for negligence in connection with the recent disaster on the Fox river.
The United States Senate went into executive session on Wednesday, confirmed a number of nominations and discussed the Chinese treaties. Mr. Dawes, who on March 24th withdrew the resolution for the election of officers, made a speech in moving the executive sessions, saying that the Republicans would not give up the fight over the election of officers.

In Franklin county, Va., negroes who were charged by illicit distillers with giving information against them have been whipped and abused. In some cases their houses were burned and the negroes sent out of the country.

Secretary Windom has revoked the Treasury order which instructed collectors of the customs to assess the duty on certain knit goods at 35 per cent. ad valorem instead of 50 cents per pound specific and 35 per cent. ad valorem.

Elder Gilbert Beebe died in Middletown, N. Y., on Monday. He was born in Norwich, Conn., Nov. 25, 1800. He embraced religion at the age of seven years, was baptized at eleven years, and joined the Baptist Church at Norwich at sixteen. He was publisher of the Signs of the Times, and well known throughout the country.

A letter from President Grevy, of France, accepting on behalf of France the invitation to participate in the Yorktown Centennial was presented to President Garfield Saturday.

The census statistics of the manufacture of glass in the United States show 194 establishments, employing 23,822 men and $19,415,599 capital, with a product valued at $21,013,464. In 1870 there were 154 establishments, with 15,367 employees and a capital of $13,826,142, the product being valued at $18,470,507. There were $9,112,301 paid in wages in 1880 and $7,589,110 in 1870.

The debt of the United States was reduced during April by about $9,000,-000.

In New York city the Grand Jury presented the indictment against Police Commissioners French, Nichols, Mason and Matthews, and against the members of the previous board, including the three first Commissioners and ex-Police Commissioner William F. Smith. They are charged with misdemeanor in not keeping the streets clean and removing the ashes.

Professor Swift, of Rochester, has discovered a new comet. The Professor does not agree with Proctor in the opinion that the appearance of a comet this year bodes ill to the earth.

John W. Minturn, a member of the firm of Grinnell, Minturn & Co., of New York, shipping and commission merchants, shot himself Saturday at his office. Mr. Minturn's health had been poor for a number of years and he had spent much time abroad. He only returned from Paris Monday, leaving his family in that city. The only explanation of the suicide seems to be that Mr. Minturn took his life while temporarily insane.

At Kansas City the flood was 'so great that a man was killed by a steamer crashing into a house on the balcony of which he was standing.

Since January 1, over 100,000 immigrants have arrived at the port of New York. During April 60,000 arrived.

Gov. Ludlow, of New Jersey, has signed the act passed by the last Legislature prohibiting the employment of more than one hundred convicts at any one branch of industry at the New Jersey State prison.

Royal S. Carr, who was convicted of murdering W. W. Marcommock, a half-breed Indian, on December 11, 1878, was hanged at Windsor, Vt., on Friday. Carr wanted to marry Marcommock's wife. He therefore induced the husband to go hunting, and deliberately assassinated him.

—There are 217 executive nominations awaiting the action of the Senate.

—The hotel keepers of Springfield, Ill., the home of Lincoln, have refused to entertain the members of a troupe of colored jubilee singers, although colored travelers have hitherto been accommodated.

A FREAK OF NATURE.—Our esteemed friend Capt. Thes. M. Lyles, writes us as follows, under date December 22: "This morning one of my laborers, while searching for a cow of mine expecting to calve about this time, found her during a heavy rain with triplets—two of them dead, the third living, all three of the usual size at parturition, and fully developed in all their parts. I communicate this fact as the first and most remarkable instance in the peculiarity of the cow that I have ever known or (I think) read of during a life of more than seventy years."

CYPRESS MILL, Blanco Co., July 28.
(Special Correspondence of the STATESMAN.)

The unenviable reputation of Bell county as the "outrage" district of Texas, bids fair to be taken from it by Burnet county, and it remains to be seen whether the latter will prosecute the offenders with more vigor than the former. The ducking of Honey, the whipping of Dr. Russell and the Dow brothers, and the lynching of Bell county prisoners are eclipsed in malevolence, if not in magnitude, by the action of some twenty persons calling themselves the "Double Horn Mob," who broke up the Methodist campmeeting on Fall creek last week. This meeting is an annual one, and this year was conducted by the Southern Mothodist Church, but has been attended by members of other denominations, and has heretofore been the occasion of a happy reunion of Christians, where peace and harmony have prevailed. I can ascertain no reason for the action of the self-styled mob, other than the devilish spirit which inspires some men to petty, dastardly actions. The impression prevails that they were drunk and armed upon this occasion. They cut the saddles and stakeropes of those attending upon the meeting, threw rocks at those who went out to ascertain the cause of the disturbance; shot off pistols, beat a negro who was sleeping in a wagon on the campgrounds, cursed and mimicked the preachers, and made things so intensely unpleasant that it was resolved to break up the meeting, which had been in progress but a short time. Among the sufferers was one of the most estimable young ladies in this community, whose saddle was cut literally to pieces, and it was this cowardly act that, more than anything else, has aroused the indignation of every good citizen. My informants are confident that several of these villains are known, and they say that the sheriff of Burnet county is a terror when he goes on the war-path. Let us hope that these "bloods" will get the punishment (which is entirely too light), inflicted upon disturbers of religious worship and malicious destroyers of property.

A Negro Conjurer Mortally Shot. Hampton Price a negro conjurer and so called doctor, was fatally shot in Franklin, Va., under peculiar circumstances. He had become hard up in his own neighborhood, and came there to better his fortune. He professed to be a conjurer and doctor of wonderful skill, and an aged negro in well to do circumstances became greatly interested in him. To this man Price said that the advance of half a dollar would secure a chain which would lead its owner to find a mine of coined gold in the neighborhood. The sum was promptly paid and the chain obtained, but its owner was not able to find the mine of wealth promised. He returned to Price and demanded the return of his money, which was refused. The town sergeant renewed the demand, but Price again refused, and enforced his refusal with a black-jack, inflicting painful wounds upon the officer. The latter then drew his pistol and shot the conjurer in the back as he was running. Grateful Slaves.
An old man named Woods, who was once a wealthy citizen of Kentucky counting fifty negroes among his assets, is now living in Cincinnati in happy dependence upon the charity of a colored man and his two sisters who were Mr. Wood's slaves before the war. It is not precisely a heaping of coals or fire upon his head, for the three negroes feel that they owe him a debt of gratitude which they can never repay. They are the members of a family separated at the auction block but repurchased at a round price and reunited by Mr. Woods under his own roof after much trouble and delay. The war stripped him of everything except their faithful affection, in the enjoyment of which he is now passing a serene old age.

A Long Island woman, being convinced that her end was near and being unduly solicitous about the fate of her six children, implored her husband to marry her younger sister. He promised to do so after the funeral, and the sister was equally accommodating, but the sick woman was afraid that they might not be as good as their word. She entreated them to give a dying woman the consolation of knowing that her children would certainly be cherished after her departure. Worn out with her importunity, they finally consented to be married at once. When everything was settled to her satisfaction she derived so much contentment from contemplating the future of her little ones that she rapidly convalesced.

A Pretended Conjurer Fatally Shot
NORFOLK, Va.—A negro conjurer and so-called doctor named Hampton Price, was fatally shot at Franklin last night, under somewhat peculiar circumstances. The negro having become hard up in his own neighborhood came to Franklin to try his conjuring scheme on the ignorant negroes there. An old negro, in well-to-do circumstances, became greatly interested in Price's prefessions of skill. Price promised for fifty cents to inform him where a mine of coined gold could be found. This promise turned the old man's head. He promptly advanced the half dollar and the conjurer gave his victim a charm, which was to point out a gold mine. The victim soon learned of the base deception and demanded the return of his money, which Price refused. Town Sergeant Oliver, of this place, last night renewed this demand. The conjurer not only declined, but enforced his declination with a black-jack, which he carried upon his person. With this he struck Oliver four or five blows over the head. The latter finally drew his pistol and shot his assailant in the back while fleeing.

PETERSBURG.
SINGULAR AND ALMOST FATAL ACCIDENT—NARROW ESCAPE FROM DEATH—LITIGATION ENDED BY DEATH—REPORTED PASTORAL CHANGE—THE PETERSBURG POST-OFFICE—REVENUE RECEIPTS, EXPORTS, & C.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

DECEMBER 24, 1881.

Mr. William A. Gresham, formerly of this city, but now a resident of Dinwiddie county, met with an accident this morning which narrowly missed terminating in instant death. He came to the city this morning and got very much under the influence of liquor. While in that condition, about 11 o'clock, he entered the store of Mr. William H. Harrison, on Bank street, inquiring after a friend. He had his pocketknife open in his hand, and was very demonstrative in talking. In turning around he slipped and fell to the floor, and the point of the blade was forced into the right side of the neck, in close proximity to the carotid artery. The wound inflicted was neither very wide nor deep, but one of the small branches of the large artery was severed, and the blood flowed very copiously until physicians could be summoned, who stopped it. The loss of blood was great, and Mr. Gresham was very much weakened by it. It is believed that with care he may recover. Mr. Gresham is about forty-five years of age and a man of family. Much excitement was caused in the neighborhood by the occurrence, the first reports being that the case was one of suicide.

It not infrequently happens that death puts an end to litigation by removing the litigants. In the case of Oliver, town sergeant of Franklin, in Southampton county, charged with shooting a negro whom he was about to arrest, death has removed the only two witnesses for the Commonwealth. Oliver, it will be remembered, was discharging his duty as an officer, and while thus engaged was struck twice upon the head with a "black-jack" in the hands of the negro whom he was endeavoring to arrest. Oliver, after being struck, shot and mortally wounded his assailant. The only two witnesses of the affray have since died—one a violent death, the other from malaria, and the Commonwealth is thus left without any evidence.

The report of the death of Captain W. H. Pretlow, of Southampton county, is unfounded. Captain Pretlow has been ill for several weeks, but is now convalescent.

franklin-franklin-1881-12-17.A5:
Some Singular Circumstances.
The particulars of the shooting affray which occurred in Southampton county, in which the town sergeant of Franklin shot and killed a negro who offered resistance to arrest, were published in this paper shortly after the occurrence. Oliver, the town sergeant, in his official capacity attempted to arrest the negro whom he afterward shot, when he was struck with a slung-shot by the prisoner and felled to the ground. Drawing his pistol, he fired and mortally wounded his assailant. Only two persons witnessed the shooting—both negroes. These two negroes were both summoned as witnesses by the Commonwealth. Three days after the occurrence of this affair one of the witnesses was instantly killed by a fall from his horse, his neck being broken by the fall. Only a few days after the death of this witness the second was prostrated by malarial fever and died before the case was called in court. This is not exactly a "celebrated case," as all testimony calculated to make the case sensational and interesting has been removed by the deaths, within short intervals, of the only persons who could have thrown any light upon the shooting. It rarely happens, however, that all the witnesses in any case are removed by death within a space of ten days from the time they were summoned to testify.—Petersburg (Va.) Index-Appeal.

At Len xviiile, Pa., the black fever, a disease as fatal as the yellow fever, has broken out. This disease is generally confined to the coal regions. In 1868 the black fever accomplished its fearful work in the coal country, carrying off hundreds of people, among them many prominent men and women. Families of eight and ten were stricken down, and in the smallest towns from five to ten inerments occurred daily. Every home presented a sorrowful scene. The oldest residents predict a visitation of this incurable disease once in every ten years. They apprehend that the case at Lenoxville will result in its spread through the northern coal region, and the physicians will find their efforts to cure it unavailing.

A return of offenses other than agrarian in Ireland in 1880, presented to the House of Commons, shows that the total number of such offenses was 3,084. Of these nineteen were murder and forty-four manslaughter. The total number of cases in all Ireland in which offenders were convicted was 694; the number of cases in which offenders were made amenable but not convicted, 420; the number of offenders awaiting trial is 155; the number of cases in which offenders were neither convicted nor made amenable, 1,815.

The Western device of a greased pole in fire engine houses, on which the firemen slide down, instead of using the stairways, is ridiculed by officials of the New York department. Cincinnati firemen respond with a defense of the pele and declare that the celerity claimed by the New Yorkers—three seconds between the first tap of the alarm and readiness to start—is an impossibility. They gave an exhibition recently, and the best achievement was twelve seconds, the men being in their rooms when the gong sounded.

Pittsburgh Dispatch.

Oil Inspector Ramsey, of this city, who was on a visit to the Far West several months ago, yesterday related to a reporter of the Dispatch an interesting story of how he attended a lynching in a Colorado town. His story is as follows:

"Wake up, Ramsey!" called out a companion of mine one morning at an early hour; "wake up or you will miss the lynching." I had gone to bed at an early hour, tired and sleepy, and had heard nothing of the murder which had been committed during the night.

"Hullo, Jim, is that you?" said I, "when does the thing take place?"

"Pretty d—d quick," answered my friend.

So, hurriedly donning my clothes, I sauntered out and found my "bunky" waiting at the door of the shanty. We walked up street a short distance, and finding a crowd of rough-looking miners around the door of a gambling hell, we pushed through and entered the saloon, where we found a Coroner's jury impaneled and about to begin their investigation. Two tables, used for dealing fare, had been pushed together, and on them was stretched the dead body of a police officer. I had known him well. He was a splendid specimen of manhood, fully six feet six six inches in height and built in proportion, a quiet inoffensive citizen, but a thoroughly good officer. On the top of the body lay a coil of half-inch rope, neatly rolled up, with a hang-man's noose at one end. As we entered the Coroner called the first witness, who, having been sworn, stated that "on the evening previous he had been in the gambling saloon of Jim Beggs, where two fellows were playing cards; during the game they quarreled about something, and both got up from the table and entered the barroom, where they both drank, and again commenced to wrangle about the bets. They made considerable noise, and in the midst of it the officer came in and quietly said, 'Boys, less noise; this must be stopped.' He had no sooner said this than one of the gamblers jerked out his 'gun' (revolver) and shot the officer through the heart." The witness had proceeded thus far, when a strapping big fellow, clad in a red flannel shirt, and with pantaloons stuck in his boot-legs, a broad-brimmed hat half hiding his dark eyes, quietly walked up to the dead body, and, taking hold of the coil of rope, said: "Boys, that's enough, come on," pushing his way out through the crowd, followed by fifteen or twenty of his companions. Without a word they walked down to the "cooler" (frame station-house), where the prisoner had been incarcerated, and, coming up to the six men on guard, demanded the keys. They told them that the keys were not in their possession.

"Hold up your hands, then," cried the leader. "Let's examine you."

The guards held up their hands and quietly submitted to the examination. The lynchers finding that the keys were not in their possession, went to a woodpile, and, picking up an ax, speedily demolished the door. The leader then entered the room and in a few minutes came out with one end of the rope over his shoulder, and, at the other end was the murderer, the noose tightly around his neck. I had taken my stand on the opposite side of the street, and could plainly see the poor devil as he came out. He was richly clad, a large diamond stud glistened on his shirt-front, and on the little finger of his left
His countenance did not betoken fear; in fact, to look at the man one would have thought the whole performance was but a joke. After reaching the street the crowd seized hold of the rope and led the victim down to an old building, where a beam jutted over the sidewalk. When they reached this point one of the number climbed out over the beam, and the end of the rope was thrown to him. After pulling the slack up he slowly let it down on the other side, and then leaned his elbows down on the beam, and took a deliberate look at the crowd below. The leader of the committee then approached the gambler and said: "Weil, Jim, yer time's short; want to say anything?"

Jim replied and said: "Now look here; can't you jist as well put a few bullets through me; what's the difference? I've got $1,000 in my pockets, and you can divide the whole thing among you if you don't hang. Will you do it?"

"Not by a d-d sight," said the leader. "You murdered a good man, and you got to swing for it."

"Well," said Jim, "go on; I suppose I must swing; this is the third man I put away, so I suppose my time's up."

He had no sooner said the words than the rope was quickly pulled up, and Jim was dangling in a horrible manner. His hands not being tied, he reached up over his head and grasped the rope, and thus released the strangulation.

"That won't do, Jim," cried the leader, and they let the dangling victim down again and speedily tied his arms behind him, and again elevated him, where he hung for nearly an hour. After it was ascertained that their victim was dead the "committee" sent for a photographer, and had a photograph taken of the entire "gang." In the foreground the committee could be seen—every face easily recognized—while just behind them was the dangling dead man, his diamonds and jewelry shining in the early morning sun, and above him sat the assistant hangman, evidently proud of his station. The entire proceedings were as quiet as could possibly be; not a word or shout could be heard. The companion of the murderer was given six hours' time to get out of town, and was most some two miles away by some of his friends, who asked him where he was going. "Oh, the boys gave me six hours to get out of town," said he, "and I am now five hours ahead of time." This was my first initiation into Western life, and I trust my last.

Westward-Bound Passengers.

OMAHA, December 12th. Through passengers on to day's train leaving at 12:15 P.M., to arrive in Sacramento December 16th: Colonel Lyman Brydges, Mrs. W. W. Wixon, H. P. Stanwood and wife, James Hitchens, Mrs. Mitchell, San Francisco; Miss Andrews, Philadelphia; Miss Woodington, New York; Mrs. Charles Bradley, San Jose; Mrs. Atkinson, R. H. Minister, Baltimore; Miss Nellie Cooley, Mrs. Emma Drucker and child, Vermont; William Kennedy, Australia; James E. Mills, St. Louis; W. E. Darwin, L. Vanderbilt, Brooklyn.

The Cincinnati Fire.

CINCINNATI, December 12th.—The losses in last night's fire are now estimated thus: J. P. Gay, $13,000; Crown Manufacturing Company, $15,000; Ault & Wyberg, manufacturers of printers' ink, $5,000. Gay's insurance, $25,000; Crown Manufacturing Company, $11,000; Ault & Wyberg, $4,500. The condition of Lew Wisby, who fell through a hatchway, is more hopeful, but it is not known yet what are his internal injuries. Chief Burkes is seriously ill to-night from exposure at last night's fire, together with watching afterwards at the bedside of Ephraim Stewart, a fireman, who died this morning from injuries received at the fire last Wednesday.

The Nicaragua Canal Scheme.

NEW YORK, December 12th.—The World's Washington special says: To morrow General Grant will arrive here. A meeting of those interested in the Nicaraguan project has already been held. Grant will be asked to accept the Presidency of a company, and there is little doubt he will do so. On Tuesday, or very soon, a bill will be presented in both houses authorizing the incorporation of the company. Bills have been drawn, and only await the arrival of one of the gentlemen who are to present them. They provide merely for the recognition and protection of the Government in the undertaking. Among the incorporators named in the bill are Grant and Governor Morgan.

A. G. Menocal, who has been prominently identified with the movement for a canal across Nicaragua, and who has a minute personal acquaintance with the Isthmus, is among the latter class. In conversation to-night he said that the present estimate would not more than turn the course of the river Chagres, and so would be entirely expended before a sale could be put into
tion to-night he said that the present estimate would not more than turn the course of the river Chagres, and so would be entirely expended before a spade could be put into the ground for the actual work of digging the canal. "For that amount of money or less," he said, "a canal across Nicaragua could be dug and put in operation within the time it would take to turn the river."

Secretary Thompson and the Panama Canal.

NEW YORK, December 12th.—The Tribune's Washington special says: The following dispatch was received yesterday by one of the most prominent business men in Washington from a well-known diplomat in Paris:

PARIS, December 11th.

Three million dollars reputed destined to influence the United States Congress and press. Thompson's acceptance is published under Lessep's authority.

This telegram was shown Thompson. He laughed heartily as he read it, and said: "It is probable that the last clause of the telegram is true. I am sure that the first clause of the dispatch is false."

"The Presidential Retiring Fund."

BOSTON, December 12th.—The Advertiser to morrow will publish an address to the public and the form of a subscription for the "Presidential retiring fund." The Advertiser says there are assurances that a fund of $250,000 will be secured, provided New England contributes $50,000, and if expressions of interest signify anything this task will not be difficult.

Trade in New York.

NEW YORK, December 12th.—The past week has been one of unusual irregularity in commercial circles, and many of the leading sorts of merchandise have fluctuated very much. Still, on the whole, business has been pretty large for the season, notwithstanding the irregularity and uncertainty in values.

Grist Mill Burned.

DEADWOOD (D. T.), December 12th.—A fire at Crook City this morning destroyed Hobart's grist mill and a large quantity of grain Loss, $50,000.

Murder and Attempted Suicide.

LAWRENCE (Mass.), December 12th.—Miss Pinkham was shot and instantly killed tonight by her paramour, Mr. Wardman, a married man with a family, and until recently overseer of the Washington Mills. Wardman subsequently shot himself and is not likely to recover. Jealousy was the cause.

Judge Lynch in Indiana.

CINCINNATI, December 12th.—The Commercial's Brazil, Ind., special says: George Scott, a half-breed Indian and negro, was lynched last night by a party of masked men, who took him from the jail where he was confined for committing an outrage upon Mrs. Allison, the wife of his employer.

Democrats in the House.

New York, December 12th.—The Herald's Washington special says: A prominent member of the House on the Commercial side says the Democrats in the House have decided to drop the electoral question for the present, and go on with the appropriation bills. They will push these till after the holiday recess, and until a quorum of Democrats arrive.

Will Remain in the East.

WASHINGTON, December 12th.—It has been decided that General Howard will not return to the Department of the Columbia, but will have an Eastern department.

The Ohio Senatorship.

New York, December 12th.—The Times' Columbus (O.) special hints that Governor Foster will retire from the Senatorial race, leaving the field open to Sherman.

LONDON, December 13, 10 p. m.—The case of Rev. Pelliam Dale, who has been imprisoned for some time by order of arches for unritualistic practice in the church of which he was rector, has resulted in his trial in the court of the queen's bench, and in a judgment in favor of the crown. There was no question as to Mr. Dale's guilt under the law, and the judge in commenting on the case sustained the action of Lord Penance, of the court of arches.

A Paris despatch says Baron De Friedland and his wife have been arrested. The latter, who is a daughter of the Duke De Persigning, grand-daughter of Princess De La Moscowa, god-daughter of ex-Empress Eugeine, as charged with forging her grand-daughter's signature to acceptances amounting to 198,000 fancs.

A HISTORICAL FACT.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

LONDON, December 13—10 p. m.—It was announced yesterday that two additional regiments were demanded for use in Ireland. It is stated as a matter of fact that there are more troops in Ireland than there were at Inkerman when the fate of the allies in Crimea hung in the balance of that sharply contested battle.

WORRYING THE BRITISHERS.

Consols have declined as a result of the nervousness and uneasiness everywhere felt as to the trouble in Ireland. Many merchants and others express the opinion that the government should at once declare it a criminal offense for any person not in the military or constabulary to carry arms in that country. More reflective persons ask how the government is going to prevent it, except by declaring Ireland in a state of rebellion.

A MONSTER CRISIS.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

LONDON, December 13—10 p. m.—The sudden and unexpected arrival in London of Mr. Forster, chief secretary for Ireland, from Dublin, has created a great sensation in political circles. Mr. Forster is understood to have returned from Ireland more convinced than ever, if possible, that a compromising and temporizing policy will not be of the least avail to pacify the country. He is in favor of the use of armed force, and that only as a means of upholding the authority of the government. The cabinet meeting, which has been called for tonight, is expected to be an unusually important and stormy one. All manner of sensational and exciting rumors are in circulation regarding the meeting and the line of policy likely to be adopted. The opinion gains ground that Gladstone will have to abandon his policy of waiting to push a land bill through parliament, and acquiesce in the warlike temper and proposes of Mr. Forster, who, it is understood, has placed the Irish situation in so clear a light before a portion of his colleagues as to induce them to side with him. This is probably true, and if so, Mr. Gladstone's position is as critical as it well can be, and demands immediate decision on his part. Mr. Forster insists that the time for half way measures with the land league is past; that Ireland is on the brink of revolution, and that the situation will not permit the government to await the action of parliament. The opinion of The Times and The Standard, and other lending journals, is that the gravity of affairs in Ireland cannot be exaggerated, and that the worst indications of months ago are not to be compared.

MASTERS OF THE SITUATION.

Mr. Parnell and his coadjutors are assuming a more defiant attitude, and their bold act in demanding from parliament the removal of Chief Justice May from the bench, by means of a resolution to be adopted at the coming meeting of the home rule members in Dublin, demonstrates their sense of the power they hold.

GUNPOWDER ARGUMENT.

Mr. Childers, secretary of state for war, has been in consultation with the Duke of Cambridge, commander-in-chief of the army, regarding the best measures to be taken in reference to placing more military in the turbulent districts of Ireland. The probabilities are that additional troops will be sent out at once. It is difficult for the most conservative to say how civil war in Ireland is to be avoided.

THE EXCITEMENT IN LONDON.

LONDON, December 14—1 a. m.—The cabinet is still in session, and the wildest rumors are flying about as to what is being said and done. The clubs at this time of night are full of members excitedly discussing the various stories as they come in. The streets, in the neighborhood of the newspaper and telegraph offices, remind one of war times.

FORSTER SUCCESSFUL.

LATER—The cabinet meeting has just ended after a protracted and intensely exciting session. After the other members had separated, Earl Spencer, lord president of the council, and Mr. Forster remained closeted for a long time. It is next to certain

that the coercive policy urged by Mr. Forster for Ireland, has been adopted by the cabinet.

Pavey and Herbert, the murderers, were hanged in Newgate prison, London, Monday morning. Pavey was convicted of the murder of Ada Shepherd, a girl ten years of age by cutting her throat.

An Indiana Lynching.
George Scott, who outraged
George Scott, who outraged and murdered Mrs. Allison, a farmer's wife, was hanged by a mob at Brazil, Ind., early Sunday morning. A special thus describes the lynching: In less time than it has taken to write this, the jail, situated in an isolated portion of the city, some distance from the depot, was reached by 1000 men, who came from every quarter of the city. At once a guard was formed around the structure, and the crowd ordered to keep back. Then twenty strong, determined men were selected by the leader, who headed them and marched to the entrance of the jail. This reached, the leader, through the wicket, demanded the keys. This was refused, when battering rams were brought into requisition, and, wielded by strong arms, soon burst the door open. The jailer was secured, the keys taken from him, and the cell containing Scott was reached. The miserable, groveling wretch was cowering in a corner, trembling with fear. He was ordered to come out into the hall of the jail. This he reused to do, when two of the party entered and laid hold of him. Being a powerful man, he resisted with the fierceness and strength of an enraged tiger, but was finally thrown to the floor, his arms pinioned, and the rope placed around his neck, when he was led out of the building. Upon reaching the yard surrounding the jail the villain made a desperate resistance, and, succeeding in freeing his arms, a desperate struggle ensured between him and the vigilants, in which the cries of "Murder!" "Mercy!" and "Help!" were uttered by him, as though the worthless dog was entitled to anything like mercy or help. In the struggle he received severe bruises on the head and body. He was finally overcome and led to a tree near the jail, when he began to cry piteously, but as he had refused to listen to the appeals of his outraged victim, who died but a few hours before, so did the vigilants refuse to listen to him. The rope was thrown over a limb of the tree, and twenty strong and willing hands seized it as it came down toward the earth. At a given signal ten men pulled all together, and the worthless carcass of George Scott was suspended between heaven and earth until life was extinct. After he was pronounced dead the crowd quietly dispersed and went to their homes. This morning the coroner cut it down and took charge of it. So ends the tragedy. Although no secret was made of the matter, no one can be found who was there or who knows anything about it.

A HORRIBLE double murder was perpetrated near Colona, Henry County, Ill., on the night of the 10th, the victims being Thomas Dilley, an extensive stock-raiser, and his wife. They were murdered in their bed, Mr. Dilley being shot through the head and instantly killed, while Mrs. Dilley was beaten insensible with a spade-handle, and died within a few hours. The murderers are believed to be two tramps who had been employed by Mr. Dilley in husking corn. Two valuable watches were taken.

JAY GOULD's conservatory, at his country seat at Irvington-on-the-Hudson, was destroyed by fire on the 11th. Loss, $150,000. The building was 480 feet in length, and the collection of tropical plants and fruits is said to have been the largest and finest in the country.

A MAIL and baggage car on the Louisville Short-line Railroad was burned on the night of the 10th near Lagrange, Ky. Nothing was saved from the car excepting two trunks. Charles A. Price, express-messenger, was badly burned.

THE Oklahoma colonists on the 14th broke camp at Hunnewell and marched to Caldwell, Kans., which is on the main road to the Territory. The troops still continue their escort duty. Capt. Payne has been deposed as leader, and Dr. Wilson sent to Washington to intercede for the withdrawal of the troops.

CHARLES MARSHALL, a noted desperado, was lynched at Belleville, Nevada, on the 10th. His latest crime was the shooting of an inoffensive old man named Jack McCann.

W. S. HOLBROOK, agent of the American Express Company at Dubuque, Iowa, on the morning of the 13th shot and killed his little daughter and then took his own life in the same manner. He leaves a wife. All his friends agree that the terrible crime must have been committed during a moment of insanity.

JOHN B. HARDIE, a United States Deputy Marshal, was killed in an encounter with moonshiners in Marshall County, Ala.

At Lawrence, Mass., Miss Pinkham was shot and instantly killed by her paramour, Mr. Wordman, a married man with a family, and until recently overseer of the Washington Mills. Wordman subsequently shot himself, and is not likely to recover. Jealousy.

GEORGE SCOTT, a half-breed Indian and negro, was taken from the Jail at Brazil, Ind., the other night, by a party of masked men and hanged. Scott was guilty of a most brutal assault upon the wife of his employer, Joseph Allison, a well-to-do farmer living in the eastern part of the county. It was rumored that the unfortunate woman had died from the effects of his brutal treatment.

MRS. THOMAS COOPER, residing near Bedford, Ind., was burned to death by her clothing taking fire from the kitchen stove; and Mrs. Louis Shotwell lost her life at Boston Station, Ky., by her clothing coming in contact with some burning grease on the stove.

A TERRIBLE coal-oil accident is reported from the vicinity of Napoleon, Livingston County, Mo. The wife of James Jones, a well-to-do farmer, was filling a lighted lamp, when the oil took fire, causing the explosion of both lamp and oil-can and throwing the burning fluid over Mrs. Jones and her two children, one a young babe, the other a girl aged 14 years. The babe died from inhaling the flame; the little girl was struck in the head by a piece of the shattered glass, which penetrated her brain, causing almost instant death. The mother was enveloped in flames, and although her husband ran from the barn, where he was at the time, and stripped off her burning garments, she only lived a short time.

Two men were killed by a boiler explosion in the Baker Car Works at Latrobe, Pa.

ERNEST A. THOMALEN, stamp clerk in the Chicago Internal Revenue Office, has absconded with $3,750 belonging to the Government.

Two more cases of trichinae have occurred in Chicago, the victims being H. C. Hansen and wife. It came from eating raw sugar-cured ham. Neither was expected to live.

The boiler in Fabel & Sons' soap factory at Louisville, Ky., exploded on the 14th, killing Phil Hempel and fatally injuring two or three others.

REV. FATHER BERNARD DONNELLY, a venerable Catholic priest, died at Kansas City on the 14th.

MEDICINE BULL, the Brule Chief, was recently accidentally shot at the Lower Brule Agency by a revolver that dropped from the pocket of Mr. Beveridge, Agency Clerk. The wound is a serious one, but not necessarily fatal.

The Keystone Vinegar Factory a Erie, Pa., burned on the night of the 13th, and three firemen were killed by falling walls.

At Leavenworth, Kans., a girl named Chadwick, aged 11, was fatally burned while endeavoring to extinguish a fire caused by the upsetting of a kerosene lamp.

A BOILER explosion at Garrettsville, O., on the 15th, killed John Langston and J. G. Durfee, and injured several others.

At Albany, N. Y., Charles A. Burt, maltster, shot and killed Kate Smith, his mistress, and then killed himself.

GENERAL GRANT and Mrs. Grant have been given a dinner by the President and Mrs. Hayes at the White House.

ELIAS McVEIGH and his hired man, named Barrett, were murdered by two Indians near Eufaula, L. T., on the 14th. It is believed the Indians were hired to do the deed.

During Mr. A.'s absence he went to the house with his ax, and by his manner greatly alarmed the lady, who seized a butcher knife for the purpose of defending herself, but the brute succeeded in disarming her. He Will Have to Marry Her.

LITTLE ROCK, July 11.—Miss F. L. Bradshaw, an orphan girl sixteen years of age, living near Wiley's Cave, was induced to leave her home by a young man named Jerome Rumley. Several nights after Rumley returned without the girl. The citizens suspecting crookness held Rumley a prisoner and sent a committee in search of the girl. They found her in an old house near Greenbrier, awaiting the return of the young man, who she admitted, had ruined her but would soon return and marry her. The citizens will compel him to marry her, as her deceased parents were among the best people in the country.

A Pulaski County Row.

LITTLE Rock, July 11.—A difficulty occurred Saturday on Johnson's plantation, a few miles below this city, in which Frank Conway was shot and dangerously wounded. Johnson's place is run by Conway. Among his tenants is a man named Palmer, who has a nephew named Walters. Palmer occupied a room which Conway had reserved, and when Conway wanted the room trouble ensued. Saturday morning Conway was arrested by Officer Lurly, of this city, on the charge of trespass preferred by Palmer, when the latter was reinforced by Walters, who shot several times at Conway, one ball taking effect in the right side, inflicting a dangerous wound. LITTLE Rock, July 11. Information from

LITTLE ROCK, July 11.—Information from Des Arc brings he details of a hellish deed committed near that place. A little girl about thirteen or fourteen years old, an orphan child being raised by a Mr. Stallings, started on her way to school last Friday morning. She never reached the school, but of this fact her guardian was not aware until at night, when, failing to return home, he found that she had not been there at all that day. Fearing that she had met with some fearful fate, he gave the alarm, and people turned out to search for the little woman all night. They hunted, but in vain. At about 9 o'clock Saturday forenoon, one Winters found the lifeless body of the poor little thing in an out-of-the-way corner of a fence. Suspicion points to two colored men as the perpetrators of the outrage, and it seems to be correct, as they have left the country and cannot be found.

A NEGRO FIEND Hanged by the Infuriated Citizens of Des Arc, Arkansas. LITTLE Rock, July 12.—Henry Smith colored, was hung by a mob at Des Arc on Saturday night for ravishing a little orphan girl named Mattie Webb. The fiend, after ruining the little thing, cut her throat, stabbed her in the side and bowels, mashed her right shoulder into a jelly, and beat her brains out with a fence rail. After the Coroner's inquest the prisoner was lodged in jail. About 12 o'clock Saturday night some thirty or forty men took the keys from the jailer and effected an entrance to the jail. They pounced upon the monster like avenging angels, dragged him out into the bright moonlight, hung him until dead, and cast his body into the river. The lynching was the coolest and most quiet piece of business imaginable. The avengers were not masked, and the people followed them to the river, not a hand being raised to stop the proceedings. The negro confessed his crime. Popular sympathy is with the lynchers. From the Republican Caucus Committee.
ALBANY, July 12.—The following has been sent to the Senate Republican Caucus Committee to night:

STATE OF NEW YORK, ASSEMBLY CHAMBER, ALBANY, July 12, 1881.

Hon. Dennis McCarthy, Hon. George H. Forster, Hon. W. W. Rockwell, Senate Republican Caucus Committee:

GENTLEMEN—In compliance with the request contained in the inclosed communication, addressed to the Chairman and members of the Republican Caucus Committee of the Senate and Assembly, we respectfully urge your Committee to join the undersigned in a call for a caucus of the Republican members of the Legislature, to be held in the Assembly Chamber on Thursday, July 14th, at 8 p.m., for the purpose of nominating two candidates to be voted for to fill the vacancies now existing in the representation of this State in the United States Senate. The method of calling a caucus by individual members associating themselves together has not been heretofore resorted to, except upon failure of the constituted authorities to perform their duty, and we indulge the hope that the honorable members of the Senate Committee will not seek to enforce the authority of the recent conference or caucus, on the ground that they have neglected for weeks to exercise the only function committed to them in their creation. Such neglect has been the sole cause of the present dead-lock. The conference or caucus above referred to was not open and free to all Republican members, because the contingency which made it possible for a large number to attend did not occur until the assembling of such conference or caucus, which then proceeded in continuous session to make the nominations. Awaiting a reply, we remain with great respect, your obedient servants,

GEORGE H. SHARPE, E. A. CARPENTER, JOHN E. GULLETTE, A. S. DRAPER,

Of the Assembly Rep. Caucus Com.

LYNCHING IN ARKANS AW.
A Fiend Speedily Punished for a Horrible Crime.
Lynching is dangerous and ought to be prevented we all admit, but if there is any circumstance under which it may be permitted, it is such crimes as that committed by the Des Arc fiend, reported in yesterday's issue of the Democrat.

Brutes of this kind, it would seem, would soon learn to shun Des Arc. A few years since the people of that law-abiding town tarred and feathered a couple of brutes who insulted a lady, tied their hands behind them and set them adrift in White river in a canoe.

The latest and most horrible act was the outrage and murder of the little orphan girl, Matilda Webb, by the negro brute, Henry Smith. The fiend, after ruining the little thing, cut her throat, stabbed her in the side and bowels, mashed her right shoulder into a jelly, and beat her brains out with a fence rail.

After the Coroner's inquest the Constable and a Deputy Sheriff brought the prisoner to town and lodged him in jail. About 12 o'clock Saturday night some thirty or forty men took the keys from the jailer and effected an entrance to the jail. They pounced upon the monster like avenging angels, dragged him out into the bright moonlight, hung him until dead and cast his body into the river. The lynching was the coolest and most quiet piece of business imaginable.

The avengers wore no masks, and the people followed them to the river, not a hand being raised to stop the proceedings. The negro confessed his crime, and popular sympathy is with the lynchers.

A DARING bank robbery was perpetrated on the 12th at Riverton, Fremont County, Iowa. Just before the close of banking hours two men, who looked like well-to-do cattle men, rode up in front of Davis & Sexton's banking-house, and dismounting, entered the building. One of them, producing a $100 bill, asked to have it exchanged for smaller bills. Mr. Sexton took the bill and stepped back to the safe to get the money, when the two strangers jumped over the counter, drawing revolvers at the same time, and in a twinkling took possession of the contents of the vault, amounting to about $4,000 in currency. Parties were instantly organized for pursuit and the telegraph was used to try and head them off from other points, but at last accounts no capture had been effected.

The action of the gang of men who
The action of the gang of men who gathered at the court house last evening for the purpose of avenging the death of Deputy Sheriff Spillman, by hanging his murderer, merits the most emphatic condemnation of every citizen who prizes the reputation of Emporia at home and abroad as a law abiding town. Aggrevated as were the circumstances attending the cruel taking off of the deceased officer, they afforded no warrant for a proceeding which could furnish no source of balm to his friends and whose only outgrowth, had the lawless project proved successful, would have been to intensify the horror of the mournful tragedy of Thursday night, and to stigmatize the town to the fatal detriment of her social and material interests.

Happily, through the prudence and foresight of Sheriff Moon, the deep disgrace which the lynching of Johnson would have forever stamped upon Emporia has been averted, and this community will not stand charged, in the eyes of the world, as responsible for the lawless hanging of a man who has been recognized as insane by a court of inquiry, duly impaneled to sit upon his case.

The failure, however, of the contemplated plan for disposing of Johnson, does not rob the intention of its moral turpitude, and should not secure those identified with the reprehensible undertaking immunity from the just censure which they have so fully earned. The fact remains that a hundred or more men were on the ground ready to lend their hands to a proceeding that would have inflamed the worst passions of the assembled crowd to the highest pitch, and given rein to a disregard of established law and authority which, if carried to its legitimate goal, would result in anarchy and social chaos. Security to life and property rests upon the supremacy of the law and its entire vindication, and any infringement upon this great conservator of the public peace should be regarded in the light of a dangerous precedent subversive of the most sacred interests of society. The community which condones an offense in this direction practically obliterates the line of demarkation between law and anarchy, and makes a concession that imperils every interest which conduces to its healthful growth and enduring prosperity. Mob law is essentially demoralizing in its tendency, and history bears out the assertion that its prevalence in any locality is always marked by a saturnalia of crime which renders the tenure of human life precarious to the last degree.

In thus condemning the unwarranted proceeding of last evening, we have reason to believe that The News reflects the sentiments of the great mass of the people in Emporia and Lyon county, and even those, who, in the heat of indignation over the wanton murder of Spillman, would have wreaked speedy vengeance upon his slayer, will, upon more mature reflection, agree that such a course could have accomplished no possible good, but would have been productive of infinite harm.

The question of Johnson's sanity or the value of his life to society as compared with that of Spillman cannot safely be employed as arguments in this case. There is probably not a solitary individual in the county who has learned of the sad event, but that deeply deplores the taking off of a man who was universally esteemed by all who knew him. But the painful aspects of the case cannot be mitigated by any demonstrations of violence in the direction of avenging his murder, and the parties who favor such a course and have manifested a willingness to execute a policy of that kind, are indulging a spirit of defiance against the law which will never be countenanced by the sober-minded people of this community.
johnson-emporia-1881-08-10.A3:
The Funeral of James Spillman.
According to announcement the funeral
According to announcemet the funeral services of the late James Spillman were held in the court house yard Sunday afternoon at 2 o'clock. The yard was thronged with friends of the deceased and his family from all parts of the county. The relatives and immediate friends occupied the steps and platform in front of the court house, on either side of the choir and Judge Culver, who conducted the funeral services. The choir was composed of portions of the Methodist and Congregational church choirs, and after singing a hymn appropriate to the occasion, Judge Culver delivered the funeral address, which occupied about half an hour, and was listened to with rapt attention. The speaker alluded to the unfortunate death of the deceased, gave a history of his life, and mentioned by name the members of his bereaved family. He then paid a glowing tribute to the kindness of heart and good qualities of Mr. Spillman, feelingly alluding to the high esteem in which he was held by all with whom he came in contact. He closed his address by setting forth the advantages of a Christ-like life, which not only fitted one for death, but made life a better and a grander success.

The body was then removed to the hearse, J. G. Traylor, W. J. Jones. D. W. Eastman, T. N. Sedgwick, W. F. Ewing and L. B. Kellogg acting as ball bearers. The procession to Maplewood cemetery was very long, covering a distance about equal to that between the Normal school and Fifth avenue. So large a funeral has never before been in Emporia. At the grave the funeral service of the Methodist church was read and all of mortal which remained of James Spillman was sadly laid to rest.
johnson-emporia-1881-08-10.A4: Edward Johnson, the insane negro who killed Deputy Sheriff Spillman in this city on last Thursday night, passed through Emporia Monday night on his way to Ossawatomie, where he will be placed in the asylum. He was in charge of an officer from Cottonwood Falls, who was joined at this point by Sheriff Moon. The prisoner was bestowed in the mail car and kept mighty quiet while passing through this section of timber. This, we presume, finally disposes of his case, as it would be criminal folly to ever permit to run at large such a dangerous character as Johnson has shown himself to be.

johnson-emporia-1881-08-10.A6:
A CLOSE CALL FOR JOHNSON.
The Court House Yard Invaded Last Night by a Large Gang of Men
Who Demanded the Surrender by Sheriff
Moon of the Murderer of Deputy
Sheriff Spillman.
The Lynching of the Criminal Averted by Reason of His Timely Removal From the Jail.
The feeling of intense indignation entertained by a number of the citizens of Emporia in connection with the tragedy which resulted in the sad death of Deputy Sheriff Spillman, culminated Thursday evening in the development of a plan to take his murderer from the jail and meet out to him by the summary method of lynch law, the penalty for his dreadful crime.

In pursuance of this program, which, it appears, had been arranged during the day, a large number of men, including

A DELEGATION OF MINERS from Osage City, who seemed to be the leading spirits of the uprising, and who had arrived in Emporia in the afternoon on horseback, assembled in the court house yard at about 9 o'clock in the evening, and began to gather around the grated windows of the jail, peering through to ascertain if they could catch sight of the object of their vengeful designs.

There was but little confusion among the assemblage, but the evidences of a WELL-DEFINED PURPOSE were apparent in the low and ominous murmur which ran through the crowd, and ropes in the hands of several parties left no doubt as to the nature of the enterprise on foot.

As soon as Sheriff Moon was apprised of the situation he appeared upon the scene and

ADDRESSED THE CROWD, counseling desistance from any demonstrations of violence, which, he said, would only deepen the affliction which the family of Spillman and his friends had already found too heavy to bear, and further assured them that Johnson was not about the jail nor hadn't been for some hours. The effect of this timely appeal was salutary, and a large proportion of the Sheriff's auditors accepted his statement in good faith and manifested a willingness to disperse. Others, however whose lust for vengeance burned more fiercely, demanded that the JAIL BE SEARCHED, to the end that Johnson might be secured if he should be found about the premises. To this request the Sheriff acceded, and a committee was appointed who went through all the cells and after satisfying themselves of the truth of Mr. Moon's representations, reported the result of their investigations to the crowd, which, by this time, had increased to two or three hundred in number, and almost completely filled the south part of the yard. In the meantime, it became known that the prisoner, in charge of Marshal Johnson, B. F. Romaine and Lee Vernon, was on his way to Cottonwood Falls, and it is reported that a party of horsemen immediately vaulted into their saddles and
johnson-emporia-1881-08-10.A7:
DESERVES COMMENDATION.

In accomplishing the timely removal of Johnson from the jail, and thus saving this community from the disgraceful exhibition of mob law which would doubtless have ensued had the prisoner fallen into the hadds of the infuriated crowd who were seeking his life, Sheriff Moon manifested a degree of prudence and foresight which reflects great credit upon him as a public official. He had heard intimations during the day, that an attempt would be made in the evening to lynch Johnson, and he promptly arranged for taking him to Cottonwood Falls by engaging a spring wagon and a crack team of L. F. Pruyne, and securing the services of Marshal Johnson, Lee Vernon and B. F. Romaine as guards. Seizing a favorable opportunity at about dusk for carrying out his project, Johnson, who promised the strictest obedience to all orders and manifested a feverish desire to get away, was hustled into the conveyance, and with Mr. Pruyne as driver, the trip was made in about five hours, they reached Cottonwood at 1 o'clock Saturday morning, where Johnson was given into the hands of the Sheriff. On the way the prisoner repeatedly spoke of his crime with exceeding regret and said if he had it to do again he would not kill Spillman.

FOR ALL THE MONEY IN KANSAS.

He manifested the most abject terror at every human object on the road, and felt that he had made a lucky escape when he was safely lodged in jail.

Emporia is certainly to be congratulated upon the fact that the demonstrations at the court house, in default of the material for a hanging, assumed the form of a farce rather than a tragedy, but the entire performance was out of character, and merits the most unqualified censure at the hands of all order-loving citizens.
johnson-emporia-1881-08-10.A8: Edward Johnson was not lynched at Cottonwood Falls on Saturday night, the cheap wind that some of the "boys" have been relieving themselves of to the contrary notwithstanding.
johnson-emporia-1881-08-10.A9:
Last Thursday evening, at about half-past 8 o'clock, the people of this city were horrified by the dreadful intelligence that Deputy Sheriff Spillman had been fatally stabbed at the house of Elbert Love, in the suburban settlement of Stringtown, by Edward Johnson, the negro who has been mentioned in this paper as having been adjudged insane some days ago, and who has been an inmate of the county jail since the early part of May, when he made a deadly assault upon Marshal Johnson and B. F. Romaine upon the occasion of his arrest by those parties for carrying concealed weapons.

It appears that Johnson had been importuning Spillman for some days past to take him to Love's house, where he had formerly boarded, saying that he desired to procure some clothing which he had left there in a trunk. Spillman, whose only fault was his indiscriminate kindness, hitched up the Sheriff's rig and taking Johnson proceeded to the place which proved to be the theatre of his

CRUEL MURDER.

Upon arriving at Love's house, Johnson's trunk was brought out of a back room, and upon being opened was found to contain, among being opened articles, four pistols and two large butcher knives. After looking over his effects and having Spillman take his inventory of them, Johnson replaced them in the trunk, and he and Spillman, together with Mr. Love, went into the yard, and sat down near the door. In a few minutes Johnson said he had forgotten that there were

SOME NEEDLES IN HIS TRUNK

which he wanted, and suiting his TRUNK

SOME NEEDLES IN HIS TRUNK
Johnson was promptly secured by Elbert Love and his brother and bound with a strap, and a messenger was dispatched to the city for medical aid for Spillman, who, shortly after the cutting, COMPLAINED OF FAINTNESS, and asked to be taken into the yard, where he died in a little time after the physicians arrived at the scene of the tradgedy. The coroner was notified and a jury impanched, which viewed the body preparatory to removing it to the court house, where the inquest was subsequently held, and the result of which is given below. In the meantime a messenger had been dispatched to bear the dreadful tidings of his murder to the wife and family of Spillman, who reside on a farm ten miles from Emporia, on Phenis Creek, and who arrived in this city at about midnight.

Pending the examination of Spillman by the doctors, Johnson was taken in charge by Policeman Page, who, with a couple of guards, and followed by a few boys, walked the murderer back to jail, where he was thoroughly searched and afterwards manacled. Shortly thereafter the body of Spillman arrived in a 'bus, in charge of Sheriff Moon, ex-Marshal Fleming and others, who bore the remains of the deceased deputy into the dwelling apartments under the court house, where they were prepared for burial. As the vehicle carrying Spillman's corpse moved slowly up to the court house gate a spirit of

FIERCE INDIGNATION

seemed to fire the crowd which had gathered there, and, while there were no noisy demonstrations, there were suggestions afloat that would not have contributed to the comfort of the prisoner if he could have heard them. This feeling, however, we are pleased to note, gave place to better counsels, and no attempt at violence deepened the horror of the dreadful affair, which has so appalled the community.

The prisoner has long entertained the hallucination that members of the Masonic and other secret orders are

SEEKING HIS LIFE,

and when arrested last May, he had tied onto his chest an old breast plate of sheet iron and was armed to the teeth.

At about 11 o'clock, Coroner Hibben, County Attorney Sedgwick and Messrs. I. D. Fox, T. C. Fleming, J. C. Burnett, C. S. Wheeling, D. Hammond and J. D. Davidson, who composed the jury, repaired to the court room, where the examination of witnesses was proceeded with, and which was not closed till 4 o'clock this morning. JOHNSON, THE MURDERER.

Edward Johnson, the perpetrator of the horrible crime, is a light colored negro, about forty-five years of age and of a grizzled appearance. He came to Emporia from Indiana, his native state, about seven years ago, and for the last two years had been boarding with the family of Elbert Love, at whose house the horrible tragedy occurred. He has never been married. In consequence of a wound received in the war of the rebellion, he lost a leg, for which he draws a pension. The peg leg which he wears has made him a familiar character to everybody in Emporia, and until his arrest last spring for the deadly assault on Constable Johnson, he had not been considered a "crank" or in any way unusually void of mental or moral accountability. In fact a great many negroes who are well acquainted with him, insist that he is a sane man, and this class of our citizens are loud in their protestations that the law ought to be taken into the hands of the people and the murderer be

SUMMARILY HUNG

to the nearest tree. As a competent jury adjudged him insane no longer ago than July 12, however, this sentiment is frowned down by the law-abiding citizens, and there seems little danger of mob law at present.

A reporter of THE News visited Johnson at the jail under the court house, this morning, to see what he had to say concerning the perpetration of his horrible crime. He lay on the floor of his solitary cell, his remaining leg loaded with chains. At sight of the sheriff and party he roused up with a half averted look of stupid indifference. In answer to inquiries addressed to him he said he felt very bad and had been spending his time praying, as he expected every minute that he would be taken out and hung.

Reporter—What made you commit the murder?

Johnson—"I believed Spillman was a member of the Masonic Order, which is persecuting me, and I wanted to make him confess it."

"Did you think he could confess it after you had killed him?"

"I did not intend to kill him. I only wanted to wound him."

"Did you not have murderous designs on Spillman when you induced him to take you out to Love's?"

"No, I had no thought of killing him until I saw my revolvers and the knives."

"Then why were you so anxious to have him take you out there?"

"I believed some of my things had been stolen, and I wanted to look through my trunk and see if everything was there.

Sheriff Moon, who was very much attached to Mr. Spillman, could not restrain his feelings, and with maledictions on the murderous demon he closed the jail and the visitors withdrew.

SKETCH OF MR. SPILLMAN.

James A. Spillman was born in Ohio in 1836, and was, therefore, forty-five years old at the time of his death. While he was quite young he removed with his father's family to Van Buren county, Iowa, where his youth was spent until about 1860, when he removed to Oregon, remaining there until 1869, when he spent four more years in Iowa, and came to Kansas in 1873. For some time he lived with Mr. Moon, who was then running a farm a few miles west of Emporia. Not long after his arrival here Mr. Spillman purchased a farm on the head of Phenis Creek, about ten miles southwest of Emporia, and shortly after he went to Iowa and married Mrs. M.A. Young, and with her settled on his farm. When Mr. Moon was elected sheriff in 1878, Mr. Spillman, not being very strong then, and wishing some employment less arduous than farming, received the appointment of Under Sheriff, which position he held up to the time of his death. He had made a very popular deputy, and was announced as a candidate for the office of Sheriff before the county convention this fall.

There was not a better citizen in the county than Jim Spillman, and no one speaks of his sad taking off with anything but the profoundest sorrow. His wife, who arrived in town last night about midnight, is almost distracted with grief, and his children are heart-broken by the awful calamity which has befallen them. His family consisted of his wife and a son by her first marriage and three children of his own.

leavenworth-leavenworth-1881-07.A2:
NO NEGROES WANTED.
A Case that Needs the Attention of the Governor.

A special dispatch to the Times from Leavenworth, Crawford county, discloses a condition of affairs in that county which calls loudly for the intolerance of the State authorities; and if they can do nothing, the U. S. authorities should be called in. It seems that contractors on the L., N. A. and St. L. railroad, hired colored laborers to go into Crawford county and work on the construction of that road. But it having been asserted by certain disorderly roughs that Negroes would not be allowed to come into the county to work on the road, the contractors went to Leavenworth and sought the aid of the county officials in protecting their laborers. To their great surprise, they were informed by these individuals that it was true that the colored laborers would not be allowed to come in the county, and they could afford no protection to them. As a consequence the railroad building is stopped for the present. This news sounds strange for the year 1881, and in a State, too, north of the Ohio river. It is a gross outrage and Governor Porter should see to it that laborers, white or black, are protected in their rights on every inch of Indiana soil.
leavenworth-leavenworth-1881-07.A3:
Negrophobia in the Moosier County of Crawford—Effect Produced by the Advent of a Few Dusky Laborers. Dispatch to Cincinnati Enquirer (Linn.) INDIANAPOLIS, I d., July 31. News was received here recently from Crawford County to the effect that trouble was anticipated, there between citizens and negroes imported to work on the new railroad now building in that section. It seems that the constructors employed to construct the Louisville, New Albany & St. Louis Railroad, called the St. Louis Air-Line, were unable to prepare white laborers, and were compelled to engage negroes. Knowing that considerable prejudice existed in the county toward the blacks, the county authorities were appealed to by the contractors to protect their dusky laborers. The Sheriff, who appears to be a negro-biting official of the bullet-head persuasion, replied that he would not be responsible for the result if negroes were brought into the county, and it was generally supposed it would not be safe for them to work there. Today the Enquirer reporter met Mr. Charles I. Benham, a citizen of Crawford County, who
informs him that, notwithstanding the threats and unfavorable outlook, Mr. Serples, the railroad contractor, had taken his negroes into the snared precincts, and now had 200 black laborers at work in Crawford County. As there are a number of negro-hating boodlums there, a collision may result, but as yet no trouble has occurred. Crawford County is situated on the Ohio River, about sixty miles below Louisville. There is no railroad through that benighted section, and one would suppose the citizens would eagerly welcome an outlet by whomsoever built, whether negroes, heathen Chince, or the very imps of darkness; but the ignorant populace have a holy horror of the dark sons of Africa, thore being but one negro citizen there, and he an old blind fellow named Archie Boone, who came with the early settlers many years ago, and in company with relatives of the famous Daniel Boone, from whom he gets his name. It is hoped the new railroad will civilize Crawford County, and banish her prejudices against the harmless Hamites. Herefore it was supposed all the negro-mobbing fools of the State were confined to Shelly County.

MURDER OF A HALF-BREED. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Des Moines, Ia., July 31.—Dr. Epps, a half-breed Indian doctor and barber, was murdered here this morning about 11 o'clock by a nuq by the name of W. F. George. The murder was a most cold-blooded affair. George met Epps on the street in front of Mrs. Polley's residence, where he was going to visit a sick girl in whom George claims to have great interest, and, after calling him some harsh names, shot him twice through the body, killing him instantly. George has been under the Doctor's care for some time for epileptic fits, and claims the Doctor wanted to put him out of the way on account of the girl. After doing the shooting he died, but was overtaken and captured by the crowd, and would have been lynched but for the interference of the police, who hurried him to the jail, where he is now safely confined. To your correspondent, who interviewed him in his cell, he said, he was not sorry for committing the crime, as it was necessary to save both the life of the girl and her child. He also says the Doctor was the only one who could help him, and knew when he killed him he would have to die too.

CLINOX, Ill., July 24.—There are no new developments toward the discovery of the parties who were guilty of the murder of the little child which was found yesterday in this city sewn up in a sock. PRISON TRAGEDY.
A Prisoner Kills His Companion and is Himself Killed by Officers in Self Defense.
A Prisoner Kills His Companion and is Himself Killed by Officers in Self Defense.

PADUCAH, Ky., July 24.—An exciting tragedy occurred to-day. Eleven convicted prisoners in the county jail were to have started at 8 o'clock this morning to the penitentiary. Between 6 and 7 o'clock there was a noise in one of the cells which attracted the attention outside, brought Jailer Edwards, his assistant Jackson and county Judge McGannagill to the scene. Two negroes, Levi Baldin and John Stewart, convicted of larceny, were confined together and on reaching their cell the officers found that Baldin had killed Stewart, having beat his brains out with a piece of an iron bunk. As soon as the cell door was opened Baldin attacked the officers with his weapon and would have killed some of them, but for their revolvers, which, firing almost together, sent one bullet through his body and another through his brain. The general feeling among all classes, white and black, is the shooting was justifiable defence. Everything quiet and no excitement.

A SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT PADUCAH.
Beaten to Death by a Fellow-Convict—The Murderer Killed by the Officers.

PADUCAN, Ky., July 24.—This city has been all agog to-day over a most brutal murder and fatal shooting, which occurred in the jail of this county at this place, a few minutes before 7 o'clock this morning. Levi Bolden and John Stewart, two colored men, the former a convict to the Frankfort Penitentiary for four years for highway robbery, and the latter a convict for eighteen months, for larceny, were confined in the same cell, and had been together for ten months.

About three months since Bolden, having in some manner obtained a small saw from an outside friend, made an attempt to free himself, but through Stewart telling a female friend what Bolden was doing the Jailer heard of the work and secured the saw. This enraged Bolden, and he swore vengeance, asserting that he would kill the Jailer and some one else, as he never expected to go to the Penitentiary. No notice was taken of the threat, though since often repeated. Who else Bolden meant to kill besides the Jailer never occurred until to-day, when the threat was partially carried out.

Yesterday the Jailer announced that the prisoners, together with nine others, would start for Frankfort this morning, and about the hour named a few friends were admitted to the jailyard for a farewell talk with them. Taking advantage of the Deputy Jailer, and his last chance to carry out his threat, Bolden, with a large bar of iron from a bunk which he had in some manner secured and secreted in his cell, assaulted Stewart from behind, knocking him to the floor with one lick, and jumping upon him, literally pounded his head into a jelly, while he crushed in his breast-bone by repeatedly kicking and jumping upon him. The cries of Stewart for mercy caused the other prisoners and visitors to cry "Murder!" and thus attracted to the jail the Jailer and his Deputy and the County Judge, who live near. They ran immediately to the jail, but when they arrived they found all still. Ascertaining the cause of the disturbance, they went to the cell occupied by Bolden and Stewart, and, calling them, asked the trouble, being unable to detect anything wrong owing to the darkness of the cell. Bolden answered "Nothing"; but when Stewart was called and failed to answer, the Jailer concluded all was not right, and, with drawn pistol, backed by his deputy and the County Judge, opened the cell and told Bolden to come out. He refused, and when the Jailer threatened to shoot him, he replied that he didn't "caro a d—n."

With this the Jailer made a start as if to enter the cell, when Bolden raised his club and ran out of the cell, striking at the Jailer as he did so. The Jailer barely escaped the lick by dodging, but the Deputy, who stood near, was struck across the breast and knocked down. In the corridor of the jail Bolden turned upon the three officials, and had raised his club to strike again, when three shots were heard, and Bolden fell shot through the body near the navel and through the head. His death was instantaneous.

Investigation developed that Stewart was also dead, and life had likely left him before Bolden ceased his murderous assault upon him. Bolden was a treacherous and hardened prisoner, and Stewart quiet and inoffensive. The Coroner's inquest justified the shooting of Bolden by the officials.

As stated, there was considerable excitement over the shooting, and the scene of the murder and shooting has been visited by hundreds during the day. In the midst of the excitement this morning, when the Court-House yard was filled with excited blocks, the County Judge had to address and explain the shooting and cause before they would disperse.

On last Monday morning a fearful tragedy occurred in Paducah, which caused intense excitement. About 7 o'clock, just an hour previous to the departure of Sheriff Sonner and posse to Frankfort with the prisoners sentenced at the last Circuit Court, Levi Bollen, a convict,

a fellow prisoner, in their cell at the county jail, and was in turn killed by the officers. About three months ago Stewart gave away an attempt of Bollen's to escape, and this caused his murder. At the hour named a large crowd was awaiting outside the jail to bid the convicts adieu, and while there the sound of a heavy blow and

THE CRY OF MURDER
caused them to alarm the neighborhood. Jailor Edwards, Deputy Sheriff Jackson and County Judge McGonnagill responded to the call, and, entering the jail, found Stewart dead in the cell, his head mashed to a jelly and Bollen standing over him with a piece of an iron bed stead. levi-bolden-paducah-1881-07-21.A13:
Paducah's Double Tragedy.
The hot blood-heating weather of the past month seems to have produced a regular carnival of crime all over the land. The newspapers are full of accounts of murder, rape and a long catalogue of heinous crimes. One of the most terrible tragedies in the catalogue of the past week took place at Paducah on last Sunday morning, in which two negro convicts were quickly ushered into eternity.

Two negroes named Levi Bolden and John Stewart, had been sentenced to the penitentiary, and the sheriff was about to start with them and other prisoners for Frankfort. At an early hour the jail was surrounded by friends of the prisoners who had gathered to bid them goodby. While thus waiting, the outsiders were startled by loud cries of "murder!" from within the jail. The jailor, his deputy and the county judge were soon on hand to discover the cause of the cries of distress. On entering the jail, and going to the cell of Levi Bolden and John Stewart, they found the latter lying on the floor of the cell in a pool of blood with Bolden standing savagely over him with a heavy piece of an iron beadstead, two feet long, in his hand. With this murderous weapon he had literally pounded Stewart's head into a jelly. In reply to a demand from the jailor to give up his bloody weapon and come out, Bolden refused to do so, and defied the officer, although he had a cocked revolver pointing at his head. The doors of the cell were then unlocked by the jailor, but as the inner door stuck he ordered Bolden to kick it open. This the prisoner did, and as the door flew open he struck a heavy blow at the jailor with the iron in his hand, but missed him. Bolden then aimed a terrific blow at the deputy which struck him on the arm, knocking his revolver from his hand. The weapon went off as it fell and almost simultaneously with its explosion, the jailor and county judge fired. Bolden fell to the floor pierced by two bullets and expired instantly. The cell where the first tragedy occurred was then entered and Stewart was found lying on the floor dead, his body covered with blood and his head and face beaten out of all recognition.

The cause of the murder of Stewart was supposed to be revenge on the part of Bolden, because Stewart had given away an attempt of his to escape, by sawing out of the jail some months previous. The affair created great excitement in Paducah.
