TRAIN WRECKERS.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LA CROSSE, Wis., Sept. 10.—A cowardly attempt was made late last night to wreck a freight train on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad at a place called Scheider's Crossing, about a mile and a half from this city. The villains had piled a large quantity of wood and boards on the track, but had done it so clumsily that the engine scattered the rubbish on either side of the track and only a few pieces remained or got under the engine, and they did no material damage. This is the third attempt that has been made to wreck trains at this crossing, and no clue has been found to the guilty parties.

A FEELING OF INDIGNATION.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

HOT SPRINGS, Ark., Sept. 10.—An ineffectual attempt to secure and lynch a negro charged with attempting to outrage Mrs. J. Parker, an elderly lady, yesterday, was made last night. A body of armed men surrounded the jail and endeavored to break in, but were met by a steady fire from the jail guards and about a hundred negroes ambushed a short distance away. Over a hundred shots were fired, yet nobody has yet been ascertained to be wounded or killed. There is a feeling of intense indignation that the negroes should attempt to defend the most heinous of crimes. Trouble is anticipated.

CAPTURED BY A FARMER.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ANGOLA, Ind., Sept. 10.—Richmond Bennett, who burned two churches in Williams County, Ohio, and who shot the Marshal of Pioneer, in that county, was captured near here today by a farmer. A reward of $750 was offered for his capture by the citizens of Williams County.

SHOT BY A MOB.
SENATOBIA, Miss., Sept. 10.—J. W. Gillenwaters, the arrested murderer of Thomas Eason, at Arkabutta, Miss., a few weeks ago, was taken from jail last night by a masked mob and shot. He is not dead yet, but is not expected to live.

CAPITAL AND LABOR.

Collision Between the Striking Laborers and Police in New Orleans—A Negro Killed—Trouble Feared Monday.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

NEW ORLEANS, La., Sept. 10.—The difficulty which evil-disposed persons have for the past ten days tried to bring about culminated in the killing by a policeman of a negro striker who refused to submit to arrest. This caused great excitement, and negro men and women thronged the levee and adjacent streets. Capt. Minor, Chief of the Labor Bureau of the cotton factors, was shot and stoned by negro women. Considerable of a panic followed, and the general alarm was sounded calling out the full police force. The negroes were massed in one quarter of the town, and, having no leadership, nothing was done with them. At noon the Mayor, under influence of some panic, called on the Governor for troops, alleging the police were overpowered. The Governor ordered Maj.-Gen. Behan to respond to the Mayor's request with such full force as was necessary, but on consultation discovered that the militia mainly sympathized with the strikers, and they were not called out. Mean-time the excited crowd dispersed, no other trouble being reported than the occasional brickbating of a non-unionist teamster by irresponsible men and boys. It was thought during the day that an adjustment was being reached, but the action of the authorities during the day seems to have embittered the strikers, and negotiations were declared off. A massmeeting of all the strikers was held tonight, when it was determined to give the dead negro a heroic burial—white and black cooperating. More trouble is threatened on Monday.

MEMPHIS, Tenn., Sept. 10.—An agent from New Orleans is here trying to get men from the compresses to go to New Orleans to take the places of the strikers, offering as high as $10 a day. The papers here advise the men not to go, and it will have effect. All here employed are doing well, getting good wages, and are not willing to risk it at New Orleans. Very few, if any, and it is the belief generally that none, will go.

A serious disturbance on the levee at New Orleans, on the 10th inst., originated in epi thets bestowed upon the drivers of cotton-floats. A police-sergeant was beaten with clubs, and fired on the crowd, killing a negro named Hawkins. Bullets flew thick around the officers, and the entire force was called to the scene by the fire-alarm. Charles T. Milliman quarrelled with Marcellus Walker in a stable at New York on the 8th inst. In the fight Walker was fatally stabbed. Milliman is a member of the firm of J. T. Milliman & Co., provision dealers.

Gen. A. E. Burnside died suddenly at 11 o'clock Tuesday at his residence in Bristol. He had been slightly unwell two or three days, but was in the city last evening. The immediate cause of his death was a spasm of the heart. A telephone message from the General's house summoned Senator Anthony and Dr. Millar, but before the telephone connection was broken a message came that the General was dead. Gov. Littlefield, Senator Anthony, Representative Chase and Aldrich and other personal friends immediately started for Bristol.

The Journal has the following dispatch from Bristol relative to Gen. Burnside: Gen. Burnside was taken ill Tuesday last, but neglected to call a physician until Saturday. Dr. Barnes, his family physician, was with him Saturday night and visited him several times Sunday night. Monday morning he was more improved, and, contrary to the advice of his physician, went to Providence, Monday afternoon, returning by the 7 p. m. train. On his return he complained of severe pains in the region of the heart. Dr. Barnes was not called till about ten o'clock this morning, when he found him suffering severe pains similar to neuralgia of the heart, and he expired in a few moments. When the Doctor entered his room he remarked something must be done at once, which were the only audible words he uttered but he was conscious until a few moments before he expired. No one was present when he died except Dr. Barnes and his family servants.

Ambrose Everett Burnside was born May 24, 1824, at Liberty, Ind. He graduated at West Point in 1847, served in the war with Mexico in 1847-8. He took part in the civil war as Colonel of the Rhode Island three months volunteers, and 1861 was appointed Brigadier-General. In the year following he was promoted to Major General. He was governor of Rhode Island from 1866-71, and since then represented that State in the United States Senate.

Two freight trains on the Little Miami Railroad collided near Cincinnati on the 10th. James Simon, fireman, was killed, and the locomotive was badly wrecked.

At Hot Springs, Ark., the other day, a colored boy assaulted Mrs. J. W. Parker, a lady nearly seventy years of age. He was arrested and lodged in jail. Next morning a party of masked men repaired to the prison with the intention of lynching the culprit. The colored people got the news and were hid in the woods. The Georgia Legislature has passed a temperance bill. It provides that on a petition of one-fourth of the qualified voters of any city in the State, the people in said municipality shall have a right to hold an election to decide whether intoxicating liquors shall be sold at any given point in the county, except with the consent of a majority of the qualified voters living within three miles.

That "Riot."
Contrary to exaggerated reports which have been circulated throughout the country, the so called "riot" at Pocomoke City, on Monday evening last, was a very insignificant affair. The particulars were about as follows: On Saturday evening, some white boys became engaged in an altercation with some negroes, and one of the negroes was knocked down. The mokes gathered their friends together and the white boys did likewise and caused them to retreat; the white boys threatened, as the negroes claim, to "clear em out" at some future time. On Monday night the negroes assembled, to the number of 50 or 60, and paraded the streets, saying they were "ready for em," alluding to the crowd of young whites with whom they had the row on Saturday night. No violence was offered, no blows were struck, and no blood was spilt. The Constable—who likewise holds the position of Bailiff—went among the blacks and ordered them to disperse, and go to their homes, which they finally did. For a time the people of the town were very much excited in regard to the affair, as there were all sorts of rumors afloat in regard to the matter. On Tuesday writs were issued for 52 of the negroes engaged, or supposed to have been engaged, in the parade the night before, and of this number, in default of a small fine for "disorderly conduct," 11 were sent to Snow Hill and lodged in jail. The magistrate and constable doubtless thought this the best and most fees ible plan of ending the case. The white boy who began the disturbance was also fined. In Snow Hill our authorities would have simply arrested the ringleaders, and told the others to go and sin no more. We learn that the eleven colored men were released from jail last night

ANOTHER SCANDAL FROM PITTSBURG. — A special from Pittsburg, February 24, says: — A few days ago Miss Craig, one of the assistants at the Allegheny Poor Farm, made a charge against Superintendent Grubbs of acting improperly toward her. Her charge was that he had followed her around the building several times and had addressed such words to her as "I love you a thousand times better than any woman I ever knew." The superintendent denied the statement, and said he had only expressed his appreciation of her as an official and that she had misinterpreted his remarks. To-day the members of the poor board went up to the place and held a secret investigation. They excluded all but themselves and the witnesses. The result was that the superintendent and Miss Craig were both suspended. They will not tell any other facts. Grubbs was a candidate for re-election and this, it is thought, will kill his chances effectually. He is a married man.

The richest mine in New Mexico, now worth $3,000,000, was originally sold for $3 in silver, a little gold dust and an old revolver.

Twenty-seven years ago Albert Paine, a young stonemason of Woon-socket, R. I., disappeared mysteriously, leaving a wife and son. The wife used every effort to ascertain his whereabout, and, failing, went into mourning. After seven years had passed she married Andrew B. Cole, of Woonsocket. A few days ago Paine suddenly re-appeared. He says that he passed the twenty-seven years on a New Hampshire farm, to which he will return, leaving his former wife in possession of her second husband.

A poor woman in New York has been particularly unfortunate, having buried her husband and seven children, all of whom died of heart disease. A few days ago the last of the children, a little girl eleven years of age, started to school, apparently in good health. Her mother following, a few minutes later, had her attention attracted to a crowd on the pavement near the school-house, and on going to the spot found her little girl lying dead.

A most dreadful dispatch came from Augusta, Maine, under date of February 27th, as follows: An atrocious murder has occurred near Weeks' Mills, in China village, twelve miles from Augusta. A young man named Charles Merrill killed his mother in a barn near her house by striking her on the head with a hammer. He concealed the body in a hay-mow until it was frozen, and then cut it into pieces, a part of which he partially burned, throwing the charred remains in a manure heap. The other portion he buried in the snow in Barton's Woods. The woman being missed for several days, suspicion attached to the son as having caused her disappearance. He was arrested and confessed the facts given. He witnessed the disinterment of the portion of the remains hidden in the woods to-day, directing the officers where to search. No motive is assigned for the crime.

Reports from Sioux Falls, Dakota, state that a famine exists there. No trains have arrived for three days, and the roads are so blocked that none are expected. Telegraph poles have been cut down and the tracks torn up in some places to use the ties for fuel. The public schools are closed and business is generally suspended.

John Butterton, a young man of North Hammonton, N. J., purchased a horse in Philadelphia, on Wednesday, and had proceeded as far on his way home as Kirkwood, when, passing through a belt of timber where some wood-choppers were at work, a tree fell across the road in front of him. The horse took fright, dashed wildly through the woods and across the fields to the railroad, and there, coming in contact with a passing train, man and horse were precipitated down the embankment together. The horse was instantly killed, but Mr. Butterton escaped with a few scratches.

Russian immigrants have domesticated in Minnesota the brick lined porcelain stove which every one who has been in Germany associates with his residence there, and remembers kindly for the even and healthful heat which it diffuses, if not for its cheerful aspect. Since these stoves are air-tight, and hence economise fuel, their introduction in regions where coal and wood are scarce is a matter of importance. It has been found that prairie hay serves to produce a comfortable heat when burned in these stoves, and machinery for compressing it has been put on the market.

A BLOODY CRIME AND QUICK RE-TRIBUTION.
The state of Pennsylvania has been stained by the first lynching that has ever occurred within its borders. Jacob Gogle and Annie, his wife, with their three children, aged respectively 9, 12 and 16 years, a quiet German family, lived in the little hamlet of Santee's Mills, four miles north of Bethlehem, on the Lehigh & Susquehanna railroad. Joseph Snyder, 24 years of age, of Easton, Pa., worked in an ore bed in the neighborhood and boarded in the family. He had frequently made improper advances toward Alice, the prepossessing daughter of Mr. Gogle, aged 16. The daughter had complained to her parents of the actions of Snyder, and her father had had several stormy interviews with him, telling him that he must either leave the house or stop at once his disagreeable attentions to his daughter. On Saturday they had a bitter quarrel, and Snyder was told that he must pay his board and leave the house. On Sunday, Snyder remained home in a cheerful mood, joining with the children and two girl friends, who had come from Farmersville, a few miles distant, to spend the night with them, in singing their Christmas anthems, which they were practising for an entertainment in which they were to take part in a few days. The family including Snyder retired at the usual hour. At 2 o'clock yesterday morning George B. Ritter, who lives a few rods from the Gogle residence, was awakened by Snyder, who said that robbers had been to the house and murdered Mr. and Mrs. Gogle. Ritter called his hired man, Hugh Sandt, who accompanied Snyder. The two stopped at the house of Joseph Santee, and they hastened to Gogle's house. In the room occupied by Gogle and his wife a shocking spectacle was presented. A prettily wrought bed-quilt was removed from the head of the bed and there were exposed to view the murdered couple, Jacob Gogle and his wife Annie, the former about 38 and the latter 34 years of age. The instrument with which the deed had been committed, an axe, was still lying crosswise over the breast of the woman, as placed there by the murderer. The sharp end of the axe had been used in doing the work. Mr. Gogle's head presented a shocking appearance, the upper portion of his skull having been crushed in, and a frightful gash had been made across the mouth. His head was almost severed. Mrs. Gogle's skull was also fractured and her throat cut. Both lay side by side, weltering in their blood.

The farmers from the surrounding country had by this time flocked to the scene, and the excitement became intense. Everybody present was so excited that it was difficult to obtain any particulars of the tragedy. Before 6 o'clock Snyder had mysteriously disappeared. From the children it was learned that Snyder had entered their room in the night and endeavored to accomplish a hellish purpose on Alice, the oldest daughter. Not succeeding in his purpose, he locked their door on the outside. Then it is supposed that he went down stairs and murdered the sleeping couple. Snyder was attired in a shirt only, and with his hands dripping with blood, he crept back into Alice's room. She had a companion sleeping with her, and as soon as he touched the bed they awoke and ran screaming from the room. He followed, and drove them and the children into the upper room, and locked the door. Through a stovepipe hole they saw him burn his shirt in the room below. Then he dressed himself, let them out, and took them to the room where the murdered parents lay, saying that burglars had done the deed, and that he was going to alarm the neighbors.

With Snyder's disappearance from the premises there also disappeared a four-barrel revolver, which was kept in an empty cigar box on the window sill in Mr. Gogle's bedroom. The revolver was owned by Mr. Gogle. Under the direction of Detective Yohe, the country was scoured to find Snyder. Every foot-print was followed, and at length Yohe, searching through the straw in Capt. Ritter's barn, caught the murderer by the leg. He made no resistance, and the detective handeuffed him and took him to the scene of the tragedy, followed by a large crowd of persons, who yelled "Hang him!" "hang him!" The missing revolver was found on Snyder. At about 9:30 a.m. Coroner Uhler drove to the house in a sleigh. The prisoner was taken into the house and carefully guarded by Detective Yohe with revolver in hand. Threats of hanging the prisoner were continuously made. The people would not listen to any reasoning. The Rev. D. F. Brendle of Bethlehem, who was present, asked the prisoner:

"Did you do this dreadful thing?"
"Yes, I did," he answered.
When asked why, he said lightly: "Ah, that is the question."

The coroner started with the jury to go to a room upstairs. As soon as he was gone the crowd entered and hustled the detective out of the way. A rope was thrown over Snyder's neck, and he was dragged and pushed to the door. The clergyman implored the lynchers to pause and addressing Snyder, said: "They will make short work with you; do you want to say a prayer?"

He answered: "No, I want to be hung. I never said, but one prayer, and that is

SUMMARY LYNCHING IN PENNSYLVANIA.

ALLENTOWN, Pa., Dec. 27. — Jacob Gogel and wife, residing four miles from Bethlehem, were found dead in bed this forenoon, their heads completely severed from their bodies. A bloody axe was found in the house, and the walls were spattered with blood. Joseph Snyder, who boards with Gogel, was supposed to be the murderer. He was caught by a mob soon after discovery of the crime and hanged to the nearest tree. Gogel leaves three children.

Joseph Snyder, aged 24, the murderer of Jacob and Anna Gogel, was found in a neighboring barn, under the straw, at 9 o'clock this forenoon. He was immediately taken back to the house of his victims and questioned as to the murder. He was cool and collected. He was interrogated by Rev. Mr. Brendle, of Bethlehem, and at once confessed he committed the crime. telling his story with great deliberation. He was in love with the eldest daughter of Gogel, aged 16, but was opposed by her parents. He believed by killing them all opposition would be removed to his suit. He had scarcely confessed before a rope, taken from one of the beds, was placed around his neck and he was dragged outside the house and hung to a large chestnut tree. After being suspended twenty minutes the body was cut down by the poorhouse authorities and taken to that institution, where it was found death was caused by strangulation. The officers of the law made a vain endeavor to restrain the fury of the mob, Detective Yoke, of Bethlehem, firing at one of the ring leaders without effect. Several thousand people visited the scene of the tragedy during the day.

TEBRIBLE ACCIDENT.

CHARLOTTE, N. C., Dec. 27.—A frightful railroad disaster occurred this morning on the air line railroad, five hundred yards beyond Paw Creek trestle, nine miles from this city. Two freight trains left Charlotte yesterday morning in sections, one about fifteen minutes behind the other. On an up grade, just beyond Paw Creek trestle, fourteen cars of the forward train broke loose and stopped after running a short distance. In the rear car were flagman Bob Griffith, of this city, and six passengers, three of which were colored. Though a flagman was sent back, the rear section being on a down grade, could not stop, and ran into the other train. Three passengers were killed and the cars took fire, burning one man alive.

FATAL BOILER EXPLOSION.

NEWBURYPORT, Mass., Dec. 27.—The boiler exploded at noon at Dodge's shoe factory, killing engineer Huntington, of Boston; Daniel Bridges, stock fitter, and J. R. Bailey, heeler. Chase's heeling establishment; Smith's heeling factory and the boiler house were nearly demolished. The boiler was thrown 200 yards into Green street, breaking thousands of panes of glass in the vicinity. Several men were slightly injured and the fireman is reported missing. FIRE DAMP. Paris. Dec. 27.—An explosion of fire damp occurred to-day in a coal pit at St. Etienne while the miners were at work. Eleven bodies have been recovered.

EASTON, Pa., Dec. 27, 1880.

Two crimes of the most terrible and most sickening character, by which three human beings have been deprived of existence, were committed within the past twenty four hours at a little settlement called Santee's Mills, a few miles east of Easton. The story is not a pleasant one to read.

BRUTISH LOV!

Joseph Snyder is a worker in the Coleman Ore Mine, was about twenty-eight years of age, a German by birth, of muscular build and not bad looking. He had lived for some time as a boarder in the family of Mr. Jacob Gogle, of whose daughter, Alice, he became enamored. Alice was but fifteen years old and her parents objected to her acceptance of Snyder as a husband. Thus there arose ill-feeling between Snyder and Mr. and Mrs. Gogle.

He had frequently made advances toward Alice, the prepossessing daughter of Mr. Gogle. The daughter had complained to her parents of the actions of Snyder, and her father had had several stormy interviews with him telling him that he must either leave the house or stop at once his disagreeable attentions to his daughter. On Saturday they had a bitter quarrel, and Snyder was told that he must pay his board and leave the house. Yesterday (Sunday) Snyder remained home in a cheerful mood, joining with the children and two girl friends, who had come from Farmersville, a few miles distant, to spend the night with them, in in singing their Christmas anthems, which they were practising for an entertainment in which they were to take part in a few days.

About eleven o'clock last night Snyder arose from his bed, and entering in a nrde state the room where Mr. and Mrs. Gogle were sleeping brained each of them with an axe. He then sought the chamber of the young girl whom he had professed to love. With her there were at the time a girl named Clara Young, who was paying her a visit, and her younger sister, Mary. Snyder here conducted himself in a shameless and brutal manner, and the terrified girls—two of them mere children—screamed at the top of their voices.

THE CHAMBER OF DEATH.

Clara and Mary, crying "Murder!" ran down stairs into the room of Mr. and Mrs. Gogle and crouched, trembling with fear, upon the foot of their bed. Hearing no sound from the couple whom they supposed to be there the strange silence increased their terror, and Miss Young, hastily springing to the floor, struck a match upon the wall. The scene which met their gaze under the feeble rays of the match was enough to freeze the blood of older and braver hearts. Mr. and Mrs. Gogle were there, but they were apparently dead. The bed clothing and even the wall were covered with blood. Overcome, almost faint horror, the girls gave only one glance, and then tottered headlong from the room and mounted the stairs screaming.

HOURS OF TERROR.

The murderer, bravely repulsed by Alice Gogle, was still in her room; but when he heard the approach of Clara and Mary he savagely seized them, and, pushing them into another room, locked the door. They remained there for some time shivering with both cold and terror. The murderer then went down stairs and taking off his shirt burned it in the stove. The girls remained locked in the second room for several hours until they were almost dead with fright and suspense. Alice Gogle, looking through a pipe hole in the floor, saw the murderer putting his shirt in the stove. She asked him what he was doing, and he replied that it was not his shirt but some shingles that he was burning. She told him that she knew it was his shirt.

THE ALARM GIVEN.

Snyder now went out and alarmed the neighbors, telling them that a murder had been committed at Gogle's house. He did not appear excited or concerned in the least, but while the neighbors were assembling he took care to disappear. This was about four o'clock this morning.

The excitement and confusion were great, and little or nothing had yet been done toward caring for the children or looking for the murderer. Threats of lynching were at once made contingent upon the finding of the murderer.

FORT MONROE, December 28.—A disturbance occurred Friday at Smithville, fifteen miles west, between a white man named Dunn and a party of colored men who had met to organize a military company. One of the men caught Dunn by the whiskers and slapped his face, whereupon he drew a pistol and killed the negro. Dunn then ran into a store and loaded his pistol, when a crowd headed by Dan Cook with a drawn sword attacked him. He shot Cook dead, after which he drew a butcher knife and cut his way out. One man named Ed. Drew was badly cut in the abdomen and will probably die, while others were more or less injured. Dunn gave himself up and is now in jail. Intense excitement prevails among the colored people of the peninsula.

AN INHUMAN MOTHER.

BELLEVILLE, ILL., December 28.—A little settlement called Twist Hill, some eightor ten miles from here, was much excited Saturday morning last by the discovery of the dead body of Mrs. Sutter, a widow, lying in bed between her two children, little girls six and four years of age, and the dead body of an infant in a basket in a shed in the rear of the house. It appears that Mrs. Sutter was confined some time during Friday night, and that she placed the baby in an out-house, where it was frozen to death, and then returned to her bad and died from hemorrhage.

MYSTERIOUS ASSASSINATION.

GLENS FALLS, N. Y., December 28.—John Shaw, while sitting at the window of his residence last evening, was shot dead by an unknown assassin.

SHOOTING AT A DANCE.

DENVER, December 28.—A Republican special says: On Saturday night, during a drunken row in a dance hall at Robinson's Camp, a man named Meally was shot through the breast. Policeman Wm. Elbany, in attempting to arrest the disturbers, was shot in the foot. Several others had bullet holes in their clothing.

MIDWAY, December 28.—Thede Lee shot and killed Chris. Lawson, his brother-in-law, on Christmas night, after being severely and dangerously stabbed by Lawson.

BARDSTOWN, December 28—An aged negro named Robert Nicholson, in a temporary rage, yesterday shot and killed Thomas Applegate, a lad 11 years old, who had offended him while visiting at his house.

Corney Anstell has issued warrants for the arrest of all who participated actively in the lynching of Joseph Snyder. He says he will do his duty fully in the matter, but fears no jury can be found willing to convict.

A DESPERATE STATE OF AFFAIRS.

DENVER, December 28.—A Tribune Santa Fe special says: A very serious disturbance exists to-day at Socorro, New Mexico, the authorities refused to arrest the murderer of Conklin, editor of the Socorro Sun, and the citizens finding no recourse at law arrested and hold by force the Sheriff and four others, including the murderer of Conklin.

The rescue of the prisoners is threatened and bloodshed imminent. A request has been made to the military commander of the district for troops, and although the troops cannot be used as a posse comitatus, yet a company have been ordered from Colorado, N. M., as a means of protection for public property and the property of the R. R. Company. Bodies of men are being armed at Albuquerque and other points in the vicinity, and will go to Socorro to-night. Grave results may be expected to-night. All the women and children have been moved out of town.

SUICIDE OF A POSTAL CLERK.

St. Louis, December 28.—The dead body of Henry Tremyer, German, forty-seven years old, was found in the southern part of the city to-day with a bullet hole in the head, he having committed suicide. He was a clerk in the postoffice, and the only reason assigned for the act was the apprehension that he would be discharged. He left a wife and two children.

District Attorney Ansett, of Northampton county, finds him elf very much embarrassed in the discharge of the duty upon him to bring to justice the lynchers of the murderer Snyder. He declares that he is the only man in his county who wants to punish them, and lets it appear plainly enough that he only desires to do so because he recognizes it as his sworn duty. Mr. Anstett does not attempt to shirk his duty, but if public sentiment is as he says, his position is certainly an unenviable one. Yet if he is a strong man he will find his account in it. It is the place for a strong man. The duty imposed upon him is as plain as the public sentiment that fails to support him in it. Of course, it is very disgraceful to the people that they should so unanimously defy the law. It proves that they are not acting under a calm judgment. The course which they urge upon Mr. Anstett now is one which will work his condemnation, even in their own eyes, but a little while hence. If he does as they would have him, they will despise him then as heartily as they would applaud him now. There is absolutely no course for a public officer to pursue, to maintain his good name and establish his fame, but to firmly and fearlessly discharge his duty under all circumstances; and the greater the obstacles put in his way the greater the credit which must come to him in overcoming them.

Mr. Anstett's fellow citizens are mad. He admits that he lost his head when he looked upon the brutal work of the murderers and asked the crowd why they had not put a pile of laths, that he saw lying nearby, under the suspended murderer and so burned him to death. We cannot wonder that a district attorney, who was so excited as to make such a suggestion, should find himself embarrassed in prosecuting his neighbors and friends, who in a similar transport, had taken Snyder's life; especially when among those abetting the crime by his presence was the district attorney's own father. To prosecute him would require a Roman virtue, which it is fair to admit that most men would not display. To bring to the bar of justice relatives and friends, and to defy existing public sentiment in doing it, calls for a strength which very few law officers would display. Yet we hope to see Mr. Anstett equal to the occasion. We trust that he will not let the people of his county escape the responsibility of dealing with this awful crime. If lynching is to be sanctioned and condoned in Northampton, let it be committed to its grand jury to say so. The prosecuting officer's duty is so plainly to bring it to their judgment, that he cannot defend himself in failing to do so.

They really undertake to claim that the lynching is sufficiently defended by the fact that Laros escaped the gallows on the ground of insanity and that Bortree is imprisoned twelve years just ahead of being hung. THE SNYDER LYNCHING.
EASTON, Pa., Jan. 6—District Attorney, Anstett's official term expired on the 21st of December, and nothing was done with regard to the Snyder lynchers. He has already stated in an interview with a reporter that his own father was a participant in the lynching, and it was not likely that he would feel like stirring to set the machinery in motion, especially as it wanted but a few days to the end of his term and his relief from any responsibility as an officer of the law. But beyond that, he was not bound to issue warrants, but to prosecute offenders who had been regularly informed against. Robert James, Esq., succeeds him, and he has given no intimation of the course he will pursue. But it is generally expected that the next Grand Jury will be charged on the subject by Judge Meyers. Meanwhile public opinion is opposed to prosecuting and punishing the lynchers. The fact is that it was not the farmers of the immediate vicinity who did the lynching. They did a great deal of shouting and threatening, and some of them even proposed to roast the careless and defiant murderer; but the men who actually did the hanging were undoubtedly Bethlehem people. Sleigh rides to the scene of the murder and lynching are now the order of the day, but not of the night, for already there is a "spook" story round about the very uncanny place. Relic hunters have cut down nearly all the branches of the tree to which Snyder hung, and hundreds of visitors have inspected the rooms of the house in which he killed his victims.

THE SNYDER LYNCHERS.
Judge Myers, of Lehigh county, in his recent charge to the Grand Jury, dwelt at considerable length upon the recent lynching of Snyder, for the murder of Henry Google and wife, the particulars of which are fresh in the minds of all our readers, and which so startled that community and the people of this State at the time. He very clearly pointed out the duty of the Grand Jury in the case. In his remarks he said in substance:

It was said first instance where the citizens of this State took it into their own hands to punish murder. The people engaged in the lynching of Snyder committed a clear, direct and palpable violation of the laws of this State. There is no law of this State, no word in the Constitution of this State, no word in any decree emanating from any Court of Justice, that make these people the avengers of the blood of the Geogles. If the members of the Grand Jury know from from their own knowledge any person connected with the lynching of Snyder, or if they have learned it from any person taking part in the lynching, they have a right to impart the information to the other members of the Grand Jury and have the matter brought to the attention of the Court. The Court said that Snyder had offended against the law of Pennsylvania, and if he had been tried, acquitted or convicted, it would be under the laws of Pennsylvania, and if his execution had followed it would have been in answer to the mandate from the Governor of Pennsylvania. The lynchers robbed the State of its powers; it was a previous wrong. No matter how great was Snyder's crime, if he had been tried, convicted and punished, with the Commonwealth as his accuser, all the people of this State would be the avengers of the blood of the murdered people. Snyder's death was murder, and whatever may be the excuses of those taking part, although there may have been evils that they thought justified their actions, they should have remembered that the method of avenging the evil was one thousand fold worse than the evil itself. The Court stated that the act of these men should not be allowed to pass unchallenged, thus giving a license to everyone, everywhere, under like cases to resort to them, and he felt it his duty to call the attention of the jury to the matter and closed by saying that if the jury does not take any action in the matter, the Court will have to institute proceedings.
snyder-northampton-county.A12: WHEN Judge Meyers called court at Easton, a few days ago, he delivered a charge to the Grand Jury on the question of lynching Snyder, the Goegle murderer. The Grand Jury proceeded to business and did everything else but take up the question of the lynching of Snyder. There is such a thing as a court getting into contempt of the people, and report has it that courts in that section of the State have been so lenient to the criminal classes that are from time to time brought before them, that the trials are but a mockery of justice, and hence the uprising and lynching of Snyder.

At Len xviiile, Pa., the black fever, a disease as fatal as the yellow fever, has broken out. This disease is generally confined to the coal regions. In 1868 the black fever accomplished its fearful work in the coal country, carrying off hundreds of people, among them many prominent men and women. Families of eight and ten were stricken down, and in the smallest towns from five to ten inerments occurred daily. Every home presented a sorrowful scene. The oldest residents predict a visitation of this incurable disease once in every ten years. They apprehend that the case at Lenoxville will result in its spread through the northern coal region, and the physicians will find their efforts to cure it unavailing.

TREATY ADOPTED.

Lisnox, March 9.—The Chamber of Deputies, after seven days' debate with closed doors, adopted the Lorenzo Marquez treaty with England. The treaty makes no cession of territory to England, but gives her the right of way for commercial and military purposes. England thus gains access by Delagon Bay to her South African colonies, which is an important strategic and commercial advantage.

A NEGRO INCENDIARY.

Caught in the Act Through the Work of a Skillful Detective, and Killed in Attempting to Escape.

Dispatch to Cincinnati Enquirer.

CAMPBELLSBURG, Ky., March 8.—For several months this (Henry) county has been infested with a professional incendiary so persistent in his work that insurance companies had denied a single policy to any of the property-owners in the vicinity, so that property in some instances had depreciated 50 and even 70 per cent. During the last twelve months not less than ten fires have occurred in the immediate neighborhood of Campbell'sburg, and not one by accident. About five weeks ago a man named Garby, a respectable citizen, esteemed by all his neighbors, was the owner of fifty acres of fine tobacco land a mile and a half south of this place. His barn contained 12,000 pounds of the finest quality of tobacco, and his new house was at that time rapidly approaching completion. Within two weeks both buildings were set on fire and entirely consumed.

When the dwelling burned some of Garby's neighbors visiting the ruins discovered the enormous tracks of a negro living in the vicinity, named Wesley Harrison Smith, a man six feet three inches in height, and as likely in countenance as the imaginative portraits of Simon Girty. These tracks were followed to within a short distance only of Smith's home, when the amateur detectives dropped the trail, being afraid of Smith's vengeance should they be discovered and recognized by him as his pursuers. Smith had long been suspected of being the burn-burner, and these tracks were regarded as good circumstantial evidence against him. Acting on it, some of the enterprising business-men of the vicinity summoned a professional detective from Cincinnati to come down and work up the case. Accordingly about a week ago Mr. Ben Hutch, of the Ohio & Mississippi Express Company, arrived here and began negotiating for the purchase of the fifty acres of the Garby land, which had been vacated, Mr. Garby fearing to erect any more buildings on the farm, but establishing himself on another farm about two miles distant. Smith's place was hard by Garby's, and to the former Hatch went, making the excuse that he wanted to learn something doubtful about the boundaries. One conversation led to another. The ill-matched pair became quite intimate and confidential. Hatch falling in with the conceited darky's political views until the black ruscal penched the whole business; told how Garby had injured him on sundry occasions, and how he was now "getting even." He said he had a way of getting even which nobody had ever been able to discover, and he had "got even," too, with more enemies than one. Hatch told him he had heard much about the burnings in the neighborhood, and did not want to buy the Garby farm if there was any danger of his being burned out. The negro assured the detective that there would be no danger for him, and then becoming more confidential, and believing his new acquaintance to be a grand ruscal like himself, proposed that they go last night and burn the barn on the place which Garby had just purchased. Hatch fell in with the plan and all the preliminaries were arranged, he to meet the darky in a graveyard not far from Garby's last night, and thence to proceed to the burn. On Monday Garby and some of the leading citizens were secretly notified, and Hatch arranged to have two of them, together with an officer, in the burn to witness the incendiary's work and to assist in his capture. At the hour appointed, the detective and Smith met in the grave-yard, and from that ghostly spot proceeded to the barn which the latter had doomed. Smith was provided with coal oil and paper. Under the barn he laid some corn-stalks with the paper, saturated them all with coal oil, and then lighted them, and just as the flame lighted up his ugly visage, Hatch pulled his cocked revolver. "You're my prisoner."

Instantly Smith was on the run, and the detective, to frighten him to a halt, fired in the air, but without effect. Then a bond was drawn, and Hatch's weapon sent a bullet into the negro's shoulder. The fugitive only, ducked a little at this, and kept on. As the first shot was fired, from the barn poured out a dozen masked men, who, unknown to Hatch, had gathered with the avowed purpose so soon as Hutch caught the darky of taking him to the first tree and hanging him. They were all armed, and while three or four returned to extinguish the flames the rest joined in the pursuit of the fleeing Smith, all taking a hand in the shooting. In less than thirty seconds after the first shot was fired the wounded fugitive attempted to climb over a fence, when a load of buckshot from one of the pursuers dropped him. He was picked up, hauled in a wagon into this place, and given a cot in a blacksmith-shop, where, at 5 o'clock, he expired. A few minutes before his death he aroused sufficiently to tell some of the listeners that he "had been a coon-hunting."

A Coronor's inquest was begun to-day, and is being heard by a jury, some of whom, I have evidence, were members of last night's Vigilance Committee. As the special train on which ex-President Hayes and his family and friends left Washington for their home in Ohio was within a few miles of Baltimore it collided with a train consisting of two engines and seven empty passenger cars going south. Two men—J. Wyman Young, of Shamokin, Pa., who was in a Pullman car which he had chartered for himself and friends, and John Oliver, the baggage-master—were killed almost instantly, and twenty persons—eleven passengers and nine trainmen—were injured, some dangerously. The fifth coach contained Mr. Hayes and family, and when the crash came it threw Mrs. Hayes and several other members of the party to the floor, without injuring them, while the ex-President's chair simply shot forward a few feet. As soon as the shock had passed Mr. Hayes, after ascertaining that no one of his party was injured, got off the train and ran to the front, where, with his sons, he was active in assisting the wounded. The most intense excitement was created in this locality on Sunday evening by the report that one Anton Kloeffel had shot and killed his wife Maria, at Big Creek, in Franklin township, this county. The facts so far as we have been able to gather them are as follows: Maria Bauchspiece, a daughter of Henry Bauchspiece, sometime ago went to live in New York city, where she became acquainted with Kloeffel, and was married to him about four months ago. A few weeks ago she returned home on a visit to her parents, (as above), where she was joined about three weeks previous to the sad occurrence by her husband, Kloeffel. In the meantime we can learn of no disturbance between the couple, until late in the afternoon of Sunday last, the 2d inst., when the wife was singing a hymn from "The Evergreen," and was requested by the husband to cease that, and sing "Pull for the Shore," which she declined to do, upon which he threatened to shoot her, reaching for a double-barreled gun standing in one corner of the room; taking it up, he placed a cap on the nipple, and took aim at his wife's head, and pulled the trigger, the contents of
on the hipple, and took aim at his wife's head, and pulled the trigger, the contents of one barrel entering the left eye and penetrating the brain, awfully disfiguring her face, and killing her instantly.

The man Kloeffel, was employed as clerk in a bakery, on Broadway, New York, and is a rather good looking young man about six feet in height. When asked why he had shot his wife, he said: "I don't know why I done it; the devil entered my heart and I done it."

Immediately after the shooting, Wm. E. Kemerer, Esq., issued a warrant for Kloeffel's arrest, which was placed in the hands of Constable H. P. Levan, who promptly made the arrest, and took his prisoner before Esq Kemerer, who, after a hearing, committed him to the county jail to await his trial for the crime at the coming term of court, which convenes at Mauch Chunk, on Monday next, 10th inst.

On the way to jail Kloeffel told the constable that he did shoot his wife; that she refused to sing tho piece he wanted; that the devil took possession of him, and he pulled the trigger, and shot and killed her. The constable says the murderer did not seem to realize the enormity of his crime, or at least assumed a self-possessed indifference.

On Monday morning Coroner C. W. Lentz summoned a jury and proceeded to the scene of the murder, who after viewing the body of the murdered woman, returned a verdict as follows: "That the said Maria Kloeffel (nce Bauchspiece) came to her death by a gun shot wound in the head at the hands of her husband, Anton Kloeffel." The following named gentlemen composed the Coroner's jury: Ed. Raber, forman, Nathan Leffler, Samuel Seiler, Levi Horn, Wm. Meixel and F. A. Graver.

The funeral of the murdered woman took place on Wednesday last, and was very, largely attended by relatives and friends. The funeral sermon was preached at the St. Paul's church, Big Creek, and the body was taken to Mauch Chunk, and interred in the cemetery on the hill. Had the poor woman been permitted to live until Monday last, she would have been 19 years of age.
wife-murderer-carbon-county-1881-01.A11:
A MURDERER'S COOLNESS.
Deliberately Shooting His Bride Because She Refused to Sing.
BETHLEHEM, January 3. — Scarcely have the murdered Geogles and their lynched murderer, Snyder, been laid in the grave than the community is shocked by a wife-murder which for coolness surpasses anything which has ever been enacted hereabouts. Anton Kloefel, of New York, and wife came to spend the holidays with Mrs. Kloefel's parents, Bauchspiece by name, farmers, who reside at Big Creek, about three miles from Weissport, on the Lehigh and Susquehanna Railroad, about twelve miles below Mauch Chunk, Carbon county. Last night the family were engaged in singing hymns and songs, Kloefel and wife taking the principal part. Kloefel requested his wife to sing "Pull for the Shore," which she refused. Kloefel seized a shotgun which was standing in a corner, took delibecate aim and fired. The shot took effect in the left eye, penetrating the brain and causing instant death. After he had committed the deed Kloefel went to the neighbors and told a queer story, in which there was some truth, but all intended to divert suspicion from himself. When the murderer was being taken from the house by Constable Levan there were such cries as "Serve him like the Northampton murderer!" etc. The murderer cooly said: "All right. Give me a revolver and I will fix myself." Taking a percussion cap out of his pocket, he said: "This cap is for me. Only give me the gun and a little time." He offered no resistance to the officer and was safely lodged by the Constable in the Mauch Chunk Jail.

On the road to the jail Kloefel told Constable Levan that he did shoot his wife; that the devil took possession of him and he pulled the trigger and shot and killed her. The constable says the murderer did not seem to realize the enormity of his crime, or at least assumed a self-posessed indifference. Mrs. Kloefel, the murdered woman, had she not been killed by he man who a few short months ago wedded her, would have been 19 years old today. Anton Kloefel, the murderer, is employed as a clerk in a bakery house on Broadway, in New York city. He is a young man, about six feet tall and quite good-looking. The couple had been married about three months only. This forenoon the Coroner held an inquest and the jury rendered a verdict of murder at the hands of Anton Kloefel. This murder, following so soon upon the Google murder and lynching, has caused great excitement in the Lehigh Valley.
wife-murderer-carbon-county-1881-01.A13:
The Slayer of his Bride Acquitted.
MAUCH CHUNK, Pa., Jan. 14.—Anton Kloeffel, who shot his young wife at the home of her parents near this place on Sunday night, Jan. 2, has been acquitted by the jury, notwithstanding the Judge in his charge said that it was a clear case of involuntary manslaughter. It appeared from the testimony that Kloeffel had borrowed a gun, cleaned it, and left it in pieces. It was afterward put together and loaded without his knowledge. The young wife was singing a hymn, and Kloeffel asked her to sing "Pull for the Shore." She kept on singing the hymn, whereupon Kloeffel took up the gun, pointed it at her, and it went off. He exclaimed, "Who loaded that gun? My God! I've shot Maria!" He then ran to a neighbor's and said that he had accidentally shot his wife, and wished it was himself. The woman died almost immediately. Kloeffel was formerly manager of the Journeymen Bakers' Society of New York.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

MARCH 5, 1881.

Last Tuesday the remains of a young man named Daniel Mix, employed as a laborer on the Richmond and Alleghany railroad, were found in the canal-lock at Balcony Falls. Mix lived near Franklin Courthouse, and it is believed that the cause of his death, which is attributed to suicide, was disappointment in a love affair with a young woman of that county. He had been very despondent for several days prior to his disappearance. No inquest was deemed necessary by the coroner, as there were no marks of violence about the body.

The Auditor of the city, in a communication made to the City Council, has completed his estimates of the revenue and expenditures of the city for the fiscal year that closes on the 31st of January, 1882. The amounts balance at $215,329.16. The tax on real and personal estate is estimated on the basis of $1.50 on the $100 valuation. The former is expected to yield $78,564.52; the latter, $24,264.60. The tax on banks and other corporations is set at $10,880; on licenses, specific, $21,959.81; tax on license, capital, &c., $16,640. The receipts from water-rents are set at $12,000, and collections from tax-lists of previous years at $21,000. These are the principal sums, to which must be added balance of $48,368 now on hand.

Under the head of expenditures $94,026.92 belongs to the interest account on bonded debt, &c.; the allowance for streets is $32,907; for schools, $12,000, in addition to $3,000 for improvements; for police, $10,700; for salaries, $8,900; all amounting, as before said, to $215,329.

Burning of the Pennsylvania Insane Asylum.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

DANVILLE, Pa., March 7—10 p. m.—The fire at the insane asylum is under control, although the Molten steamer is still playing, and the fire is confined to the building, which is a total wreck. After the inmates had been removed they were placed in temporary quarters in outbuildings, and the male inmates were transferred to the west wing, which escaped with slight damage. The female inmates will be provided for at another institution. Arrangements have been made to-day by Superintendent Schultz for the removal of one hundred to the asylum at Warren, Pa. Until the removal they will be quartered in the wash house and bakery, where they are now in charge of keepers. The first report sent out that a number of inmates had perished, was eroneous. All the inmates are now accounted for. Their removal from the burning building was accomplished with great trouble. When four hundred and fifty people, among whom were a large number of uncontrollable maniacs, were safely removed, it seems almost miraculous, as the building had many long dark hallways through which the inmates were taken before reaching the open air. The patients fought desperately against removal from their wards, considering it a great treat, and some of the keepers were roughly handled. The inmates were finally removed by main force. The fire originated in a room in one of the female wards, and was said to have been caused by combustion paint and rags in an unoccupied room. The hospital was a substantial stone structure, length, 1100 feet; cost of buildings destroyed about $600,000; insurance, $250,000; distributed among a large number of companies. The fire was visited to day by thousands of people.

INHUMAN OUTRAGE.
an by Disguised Plenks in Virginia.
By Trilogue to New York Herald.

RICHMOND, March 8.—Intelligence has just been received in this city of the recent perpetration of a singular and horrible outrage by unknown and disguised parties in the Goose Creek neighborhood of Bedford County. It appears that the indignation of the parties in question was aroused by the open and scandalous relations existing between a colored blacksmith named William Jones and a white woman, whose name, out of regard to respectable family connections, is suppressed. The intimacy between these persons had gone on to the extent that a child was born to the woman, of which the negro, or at least some negro, was the undoubted parent. Scandalized by this state of affairs and by the boldness with which the shame of the misegonators was publicly avowed, a party of persons called on them both after nightfall recently and visited on each of them, but especially on the female, punishment and warning or the most barbarous character. The negro was given a terrible whipping, which he is said to have received with great resignation, in view of the report that no worse thing betoll him. The woman was visited by a bodily and manness injury, intended to express in a very emphatic and awful manner the condemnation in which her mode of life was regarded by the community. It was necessary for her to seek the skilled services of a smith to relieve her from the inhumane consequences of the masked men's visit. Whether the maskers were white or black is not known, though in the terror inspired by the occurrence the negroes in the neighborhood generally reported that the Klu Klux had done it. As there are not, and never have been, any Klu Klux in this or in any section of Virginia, it is evident that they merely employ the term to describe the maskers and the mysterious way in which this outrage altogether without parallel in Virginia, was perpetrated in the law-abiding County of Bedford.

WASHINGTON, December 9th.—It is reported that the President's Message, with reference to the South American question, does not read at all like the manuscript furnished by Blaine as the views of the state Department on the subject. The troubles with the cow-boys on the Mexican border also received attention, and it is believed that some action will soon be taken to protect the frontiers both of the United States and Mexico from depredations by this class of marauders.

Further Congressional Gossip.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 9.—Speaker Keifer said to-day that nothing had yet been done in regard to the Committee Chairmanships of the House, which might not be as well done to-morrow. As to the composition of the committees he maintains great reticence. The impression prevails that he will announce them next week, but there is no authority from him for the statement. It is thought very probable, however, that, in view of the acknowledged complications surrounding the Utah case, the Speaker will announce the Committees on Elections on Tuesday, so that the contest may be taken in hand by that committee without delay.

That Disgusting Hurricane.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 9th.—D. McLean Shaw testified in the Guiteau case that the prisoner told him that he was bound to have notoriety somehow or other. He might kill some big man and imitate Wild and Booth. At this the prisoner became very violent and abusive.

Money and stocks.

New York, Dec. 9th.—Silver bars, 112$\frac{3}{4}$; money, 2 to 1$\frac{1}{4}$ per diem; governments strong and higher; stocks dull; Western Union, 85$\frac{1}{8}$; Quicksilver, 13; Pacific, 44$\frac{5}{8}$; Mariposa, 2$\frac{1}{4}$; Wells, Fargo, 134; New York Central, 139$\frac{1}{4}$; Erie, 45$\frac{5}{8}$; Panama, 195; Union Pacific, 119$\frac{1}{4}$; bonds, 117$\frac{1}{4}$; Central Pacific, 94$\frac{1}{2}$; bonds, 115$\frac{1}{2}$; Sutro, 1$\frac{1}{8}$.

A "Gone" Nigger.

Montgomery, Ala., Dec. 9th.—A few nights ago Wm. McCann, a merchant in Chambers county, was called up by some negroes and as soon as he opened the door was killed. The negro who confessed the crime was lodged in the Lafayette jail and it is expected that he has been lynched, as a great crowd was seen on its way to the jail.

A Murderer swings.

LITTLE ROCK, Dec. 9th.—Frank Hall, colored, was executed at noon to-day, for the murder of Paul Saunders, two years ago.

Decency on the scaffold—A Controfe Criminal.

MONTREAL, Dec. 9th.—Hugh Hayvern was executed in the jail yard this morning, for the murder of Wm. Salton, a fellow convict in the penitentiary. He was very contrite.

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

CHARLESTON, W. VA., November 16.—William Robinson, a notoriously bad man, a citizen of Malden, six miles above this place, shot and instantly killed Allen Bilcher, town marshal, last evening, who was trying to arrest him. Robinson also shot twice at D. H. Putney, mayor. He is now in jail here. Some fears are entertained that there may be another court of Judge Lynch.

A Murderer's Life in Danger.
On Tuesday evening William Robinson, a notorious character of Malden, six miles above Charleston, West Virginia, shot Town Marshal Allen Belcher through the heart. Belcher died instantly. Robinson also shot twice at the Mayor, but missed him. The murderer is in jail and there is much excitement with fears of lynching, which is freely talked of. It is reported that a mob is coming from Malden to take Robinson from the jail and hang him. Colonel Appleton has rendered the Hale Rifflemen to be ready for the protection of the jail.

THE KANAWHA TROUBLES.
The State Troops on the Ground-Fears of Mob Work.
Special Dispatch to the Intelligencer.
CHARLESTON, November 19.—Colonel Appleton, in charge of the State troops in the Valley, informed me that nothing new has developed at Coal Valley to-day. The Hawk's Nest company of militia is on the ground, and the company from Hinton will be there to-night. There is great danger of an outbreak to-night, and Sheriff Tyres is very much excited. Will keep you posted on developments. The United States Marshal at Hinton is guarding the Charleston jail to prevent an attack from a mob, which is supposed to be organizing on Campbell's creek for the purpose of lynching Robinson, who murdered Allen Belcher a few days ago, in Malden.

Two atrocious murders have been committed in Kanawha county during the past week. Last Saturday night three drunken men, Henry Reynolds, Scott Harmon and George Pack, met at the house of the latter, about two miles above Charleston, on the south side of the Kanawha. Pack and Reynolds were half-brothers. Reynolds picked the banjo while the others danced. A woman named Medley, a sweetheart of Reynolds, was present and wanted to dance. Reynolds, being jealous of the other men, objected. A quarrel ensued in the midst of which Pack drew a pistol and shot Reynolds dead in his tracks.

Tuesday afternoon, in the notorious town of Walden, occurred

The Second Murder.

Allen Belcher, formerly justice of the district, and a descent, respectable man, has for some time been Marshal of the town. He has tried faithfully and bravely to suppress a few roughs who have infested the place. Among them was Wm. H. Robinson, a drunken ruffian, the terror of the whole village. A short time ago he shot at Henry Spriegel, and came near killing him. Later he fell upon John Brown with a knife and hewed and hacked him within an inch of his life. Brown is living, but terribly malmed.

Robinson was released on bail a few weeks ago. Tuesday he went to Malden and proceeded to occupy the place—defying the authorities and threatening to kill Marshal Belcher if he obstructed him. Belcher attempted to arrest him, and Robinson shot at him as he prepared to advance. Belcher dropped dead, Robingon's bullet having penetrated his heart. The murderer was arrested and confined in the Charleston

G. BARTH, of Napa, Cal., has fled to Arizona with $30,000 of trust funds.

It is discovered that J. Howard Wells, Jay Gould's blackmailer, is a commissary who defrauded the government out of about $2,000,000 and then went to Europe during the war.

A son of Rev. Dr. Lanahan, pastor of the Foundry Methodist church of Washington, was arrested in the postoffice at Baltimore for embezzling money from the mails.

Joseph GREEN, a young lawyer of New Orleans, attempted to fight a duel with Gutheim, a son of the leading rabbi of that city, in the lower park, but the principals and seconds were bagged by the police and locked up.

At Scandia, Kan., Dr. W. H. Woodward was mortally shot by J. C. Humphrey, editor of The Telescope. The affray grew out of a local political contest, and there are threats of lynching.

Two adventurers whose fathers are merchants in Pittsburg were found secreted in a through mail car at Steubenville, O. They fought vigorously against being arrested, but were finally stowed away in ail.

At Madden, West Va., a desperado named Robinson, shot Marshal Allen Belcher through the heart, and fired three times at the mayor. A mob collected to lynch the murderer, and the state riflemen were placed on guard around Charleston jail.

The five men who robbed Jesse Baldwin, of Boardman, O., of $30,000 in gold, took a train at Columbia and rode to Pittsburg. As they carried no baggage, it is believed that the coin was buried near the scene of the robbery.

BELLE SPAULDING, who has been on trial for several days at Galesburg, Ill., for the murder of her husband, has been acquitted. The jury, which held that the killing was justifiable, was invited by "Miss" Spaulding to an oyster supper after the verdict was rendered. Eight of them accepted. The lady will be married at an early day, it is said.

6. The man arrosted at Grand Island, Neb., for murders in Pepin county, Wis., admitted to reporters at St. Paul that he was Edward Maxwell, who killed the Coleman brothers. He stated that, while besieged in the Eau Galle woods, he and his brother Lon went eighty-five hours without food. He will be taken from Menomonee to Durand, Wis., to await trial.

J. Howard WELLES, who attempted to extort information from Jay Gould about the stock market, is a nervous wreck. He occupies a cell in the Tombs, and begged hard to be allowed to retain his penknife. So peculiar is the case that it is believed he can only be punished with a year's imprisonment and fined $500. A Chicago gentleman writes to the Times that Welles was a commissary of subsistence at Baltimore during the war, and bled the contractors mercilessly.

THE ATTEMPT TO KILL GUITEAU.—The attempt made to kill the assassin Guiteau on Saturday afternoon last, while he was returning from the Criminal Court in the prison van, deserves remarks the Baltimore Sun, to be denounced by every one who desires that justice shall be done to this great criminal through the proper tribunal and by the legal processes provided for such cases. Guiteau is in the hands of the law, and the law should be allowed to take its course. Of sympathy with him there is not a particle anywhere. The act that has given him a dreadful notoriety has caused profound indignation to be expressed against him both at home and abroad. Nevertheless if he were thrice steeped in crime he is entitled to a fair trial, and that justice will be done to him by the court before which he is arraigned no one need doubt. When, therefore, a private person undertakes, from a spirit of revenge or from a passion for notoriety, to assume the office of both judge and executioner, he not only violates the law to which, in common with all others, he is bound to yield obedience, but in this case he casts a stain upon the honor of the nation. Dierkman's Dark Deeds.
St. Louis, March 17.—On Monday evening last William Dierkman had an altercation which led to a fight with his employer, Henry W. Mertz, at Hilltown, twenty miles west of this city, and the former stabbed the latter in the abdomen and thigh, the wounds resulting in his death last night. Dierkman was arrested and lodged in jail. The affair created a good deal of excitement, and reports have reached this city that the neighbors of Mertz, and others living in that part of the country, gathered at Hilltown this morning with the determination of lynching Dierkman. The case is aggravated by the fact that Dierkman's wife was murdered two years ago, and although a man named Stoeckli was convicted of the crime, there are many who believe that Dierkman was the real murderer, and they are greatly incensed against him.

POSSIBLY A LYNCHING.
Kenry Mertz Dies From the Wound Inflicted by Dieckmaa.
t. Louis Post-Dispatch

Henry Mertz, the postmaster at Hilltown on the Oliyer street road, who was cut three days ago by William Dieckman, died of the wound about four o'clock this morning. The gash was a frightful one, in the groin, and the case was recognized as hopeful from the first call of the physician. The particulars were generally known throughout the western part of the county, and there has been developing a good deal of feeling against Dieckman. The latter will be remembered as the farmer whose wife was murdered at Hog Hollow two years ago. Dieckman was at first suspected of complicity in the tragedy, but afterward suspicion fastened on Joe Stoeckkli who has been tried twice.

When the Post-Dispatch messenger left Hilltown this morning there was a strong prospect that Dieckman would not live to see the sun go down. He was captured some hours after the cutting of Mertz and locked up in the Clayton jail. Preparations were commenced this morning for holding the inquest, both 'Squire Fischer and 'Squire Reaves being notified of the need of their services. Hilltown is twenty miles from St. Louis and off the line of any railroad. The news of Mertz's death, however, spread, and the farmers commenced gathering from all the surrounding country. There were between seventy-five or a hundred of the yeomanry at Hilltown and at Lake post-office when the messenger left, and there seemed to be but one sentiment—Dieckman was observing of death, and might as well suffer the penalty without delay.

Oustable Kessler and his deputy, Jake Berg, were reported to have started for Clayton to bring out the prisoner, and were expected to return to Hilltown with him about noon. There was a report that one body of men numbering fifty would be up from Manchester and Baldwin by the time the prisoner arrived, and the more hot-headed were in favor of taking Dieckman from the posse when he reached Lake postoffice and lynching him before the inquest. Others counseled, waiting for the verdict, promising that if there were no mitigating circumstances there should be no delay in executing vengeance.

Dieckman threatened to murder before the cutting. He was seen sharpening his knife very carefully in the afternoon, and dropped the significant remark as he felt the edge, "This will bring blood."

Special to the Herald.

St. Louis. July 1.—Wm. Keokman has been on trial for the past four days at Clayton, the county seat of St. Louis county, for killing Henry Mertz. The case was given to the jury yesterday and at a late hour last night they returned a verdict of murder in the second degree, assessing the punishment 18 years in the penitentiary. The crime was committed on the 14th of March and the killing was done with a knife.

Charles King, Joseph Kotousky and Charles Ellis are in the St. Louis jail awaiting the execution of the death penalty assessed against them. These three men are to be hanged on the 15th inst., and all for killing a woman. It is pretty certain two of them will hang. Kotousky's lawyers say they have found a new point which they claim will save their client. The three murderers all seem hopeful.

There was a double railroad collision at Webster Grove, a suburb of St. Louis, on the Missouri Pacific road last night. Just how they occurred it is impossible to ascertain. The net result is a double wreck. Both of the colliding trains were freights, and there were no lives lost.

The St. Louis bakers are preparing for a strike. They are pretty generally satisfied with their wages, but say their hours of labor are too long.
